fuentes/real-cedula-del-virreinato-1777/.texto: Royal decree establishing the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

On August 1, 1776, Charles III named Pedro de Cevallos viceroy and captain general of a new viceroyalty, on a provisional basis, for as long as his expedition against the Portuguese lasted. The royal decree of October 27, 1777 made it permanent, with its capital in Buenos Aires and jurisdiction over the governorships of Buenos Aires, Paraguay and Tucumán, the corregimiento of Cuyo, separated from Chile, and the provinces of Charcas, with Potosí, separated from the Viceroyalty of Peru.
It brought under a single authority based in Buenos Aires Upper Peru, Tucumán, Cuyo, Paraguay and the Banda Oriental, the territory from which Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay would emerge.

fuentes/tratado-de-san-ildefonso-1777/ti.texto: Preliminary Treaty of Limits of San Ildefonso

fuentes/tratado-de-san-ildefonso-1777/re.texto: Treaty signed on October 1, 1777, at the Palace of La Granja de San Ildefonso, after Cevallos’s campaign. Portugal recognized as Spanish the Colonia del Sacramento, the Eastern Missions and navigation of the Río de la Plata, and Spain returned the island of Santa Catarina. The interior boundaries were left to demarcation commissions, which never finished their work.

fuentes/tratado-de-san-ildefonso-1777/po.texto: It ended almost a century of disputes over the Colonia del Sacramento and left the Banda Oriental in Spanish hands. The demarcation commissions brought Félix de Azara to the Río de la Plata.

fuentes/reglamento-de-comercio-libre-177.texto: Regulations and royal tariffs for free trade from Spain to the Indies

Regulation of October 12, 1778 that allowed a number of Spanish and American ports, among them Buenos Aires and Montevideo, to trade directly with one another, without the fleet system or the mandatory stop in Cádiz. It set lower tariffs and favored Spanish products; trade with other nations remained prohibited.
It made Buenos Aires a legal port for silver from Upper Peru and for trade with Spain, and it was the basis for the growth of its merchants, who in 1794 got their own Consulado.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1782/ti.texto: Royal ordinance of army and provincial intendants of the Viceroyalty of Buenos Aires

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1782/so.texto: Book printed in Madrid in 1782 (276 articles)

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1782/re.texto: Ordinance of January 28, 1782 that replaced governors and corregidores with intendants appointed by the king, with powers over justice, policing, public finance and war. With the 1783 adjustment the viceroyalty was divided into eight intendancies (Buenos Aires, Paraguay, Córdoba del Tucumán, Salta del Tucumán, Potosí, Charcas, Cochabamba and La Paz), and military governments were set up in Montevideo, the Missions, Moxos and Chiquitos.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1782/po.texto: It is the basis of the territorial division the provinces inherited: the Córdoba intendancy included Cuyo and La Rioja, and the Salta intendancy covered Jujuy, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero and Catamarca.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1782/le.texto: Printed edition of the period (Internet Archive)

fuentes/real-cedula-del-consulado-1794/t.texto: Royal decree establishing the Consulado of Buenos Aires

fuentes/real-cedula-del-consulado-1794/r.texto: Royal decree of January 30, 1794 that created a consulado in Buenos Aires, both a court for disputes between merchants and a board charged with promoting agriculture, industry and trade. It was made up of elected merchants and a perpetual secretary appointed by the king, a post held by Manuel Belgrano.

fuentes/real-cedula-del-consulado-1794/p.texto: It was the first institution of its own for the merchants of Buenos Aires, and the forum from which Belgrano spread enlightened political economy.

fuentes/memorias-del-consulado-belgrano/.texto: Belgrano’s memoirs to the Consulado of Buenos Aires
Memoirs read before the Consulado’s board

As secretary, Belgrano had to read a memoir before the Consulado’s board each year. In the first, from 1796, titled “General Means of Promoting Agriculture, Encouraging Industry and Protecting Commerce in an Agricultural Country,” he presented agriculture as the basis of the country’s wealth and called for technical education, roads and local processing of raw materials before they were exported. In others he proposed drawing and navigation schools, which the Consulado opened in 1799, and free schools for girls.
They are the first program of political economy written in Buenos Aires, influenced by the Physiocrats and by Spanish Enlightenment reformism.

fuentes/telegrafo-mercantil/titulo.texto: Telégrafo Mercantil, Rural, Político-Económico e Historiógrafo del Río de la Plata (Mercantile, Rural, Political-Economic and Historiographic Telegraph of the Río de la Plata)

fuentes/telegrafo-mercantil/soporte.texto: Periodical printed at the Real Imprenta de Niños Expósitos

fuentes/telegrafo-mercantil/resumen.texto: The first printed periodical in Buenos Aires, published between April 1, 1801 and October 17, 1802 with the permission of Viceroy Avilés. It carried articles on trade, agriculture, geography and the history of the provinces, news from Europe and poems, such as Manuel José de Lavardén’s ode to the Paraná, and it had the collaboration of Belgrano and other Enlightenment figures.

fuentes/telegrafo-mercantil/por_que_impo.texto: It inaugurated periodical publishing in the Río de la Plata and shows the topics debated by the enlightened elite of the viceroyalty.

fuentes/telegrafo-mercantil/leer.1.titul.texto: Facsimile reprint by the Junta de Historia y Numismática Americana, 1914 (Internet Archive)

fuentes/oda-al-parana/titulo.texto: Ode to the Majestic Paraná River

fuentes/oda-al-parana/soporte.texto: Poem published in the Telégrafo Mercantil

fuentes/oda-al-parana/resumen.texto: Neoclassical ode that presents the Paraná River as a deity crossing the territory and foretelling prosperity for trade and agriculture along its banks. It was published in the first issue of the Telégrafo Mercantil, in April 1801.

fuentes/oda-al-parana/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the first poems written in Buenos Aires that take the landscape of the Río de la Plata as their subject.

fuentes/semanario-de-agricultura/titulo.texto: Semanario de Agricultura, Industria y Comercio

fuentes/semanario-de-agricultura/resumen.texto: Periodical published by Vieytes from September 1, 1802 until early 1807, when it was interrupted by the second British invasion. It spread farming and livestock techniques, soap making and other industries, and the idea that the country’s wealth lay in working the land; it translated and summarized European economic writers.

fuentes/semanario-de-agricultura/por_que.texto: It was the main vehicle for Physiocratic ideas and practical economics among the Creoles who later carried out the revolution.

fuentes/memoria-rural-azara/titulo.texto: Memoir on the Rural State of the Río de la Plata in 1801

fuentes/memoria-rural-azara/resumen.texto: Report written by Azara at the end of his work as a boundary demarcator. It describes cattle raising and the estancias of the countryside, cattle rustling and smuggling, the frontier with Indigenous peoples and the situation of the Guaraní in the missions, and proposes granting land in ownership to poor settlers on the frontier to keep them in place and defend it.

fuentes/memoria-rural-azara/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the most complete descriptions of the rural Río de la Plata at the end of the colonial period and an antecedent of the debates over land distribution.

fuentes/diario-de-reconocimiento-azara/t.texto: Journal of a Survey of the Guard Posts and Forts on the Buenos Aires Frontier

fuentes/diario-de-reconocimiento-azara/s.texto: Travel journal; published by Pedro de Angelis in his Colección de obras y documentos

fuentes/diario-de-reconocimiento-azara/r.texto: Journal of the tour Azara made in 1796, commissioned by Viceroy Melo, of the guard posts and forts on the southern frontier of Buenos Aires. It notes distances, water places, lands and the state of the defenses, and proposes moving the frontier line further south.

fuentes/diario-de-reconocimiento-azara/p.texto: It shows how viceregal authorities saw the frontier with the Indigenous peoples of the pampas at the end of the 18th century.

fuentes/viajes-por-la-america-meridional.texto: Four-volume book with atlas, edited by Charles-Athanase Walckenaer

Work in which Azara gathered what he had observed over twenty years of travel through Paraguay and the Río de la Plata: the climate, rivers, animals and plants, Indigenous peoples and the Spanish and mestizo population. It was published in French in Paris in 1809, with notes by Georges Cuvier on the quadrupeds.
For decades it was the main scientific description of the region, and Darwin cited it.
First volume of the 1809 French edition (Internet Archive)

fuentes/sentencia-contra-tupac-amaru/tit.texto: Sentence against Túpac Amaru II and his family

fuentes/sentencia-contra-tupac-amaru/aut.texto: José Antonio de Areche, visitador general of Peru

fuentes/sentencia-contra-tupac-amaru/res.texto: Sentence handed down in Cusco on May 15, 1781 by the visitador José Antonio de Areche. It condemned Túpac Amaru to watch his wife, his son Hipólito and other relatives and captains die, and then to be dismembered. It also banned the wearing of Inca dress, Inca performances and other customs, and ordered the seizure of copies of the Royal Commentaries of the Inca by Garcilaso.

fuentes/sentencia-contra-tupac-amaru/por.texto: It shows the harshness of the repression and the Crown’s attempt to erase the memory of the Incas as a political banner.

fuentes/dilatado-cautiverio/titulo.texto: The Long Captivity under Spanish Rule

fuentes/dilatado-cautiverio/resumen.texto: Memoirs of Túpac Amaru II’s half brother, published in Buenos Aires in 1825. They recount the 1780 rebellion, the repression of the family, the transfer of the condemned to Spain and almost forty years of imprisonment, mostly in Ceuta.

fuentes/dilatado-cautiverio/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the few written testimonies by a member of Túpac Amaru’s family, and a document of how independent governments used the memory of the Incas.

fuentes/trial-of-whitelocke/resumen.texto: Printed version of the court-martial held at the Chelsea Hospital between January 28 and March 15, 1808. It reproduces the charges, the testimony of officers about the attack on Buenos Aires on July 5, 1807 and the capitulation, and the sentence that removed Whitelocke from the army as unfit to serve the king.

fuentes/trial-of-whitelocke/por_que_impo.texto: It is the most detailed British source on the second invasion and the defense of Buenos Aires.

fuentes/trial-of-popham/resumen.texto: Printed report of the court-martial that tried Home Popham in March 1807 for leaving the Cape of Good Hope without orders to attack the Río de la Plata. It includes Popham’s defense, which invoked British plans for Spanish America, and the sentence that severely reprimanded him.

fuentes/trial-of-popham/por_que_importa.texto: It shows that the first invasion was Popham’s initiative and how it was debated in London.

fuentes/sucinta-memoria-1807/titulo.texto: Brief Account of the Second Invasion of Buenos Aires

fuentes/sucinta-memoria-1807/resumen.texto: Account printed in 1808 of the second invasion, from the arrival of the British fleet at the end of June 1807 to the defense of July 5 and the celebrations that followed. It praises the role of the residents and the militias.

fuentes/sucinta-memoria-1807/por_que_imp.texto: It is an early example of the patriotic memory of the invasions, written in the heat of victory.

fuentes/memorias-curiosas-beruti/soporte.texto: Manuscript; published in the Biblioteca de Mayo (1960) and in full in 2001

fuentes/memorias-curiosas-beruti/resumen.texto: Chronicle kept by Juan Manuel Beruti for more than sixty years. From the late 18th century he noted, year by year, what he saw or heard: the British invasions, the May Week, festivities, executions, prices and city life.

fuentes/memorias-curiosas-beruti/por_que.texto: It is one of the most widely used direct accounts of life in Buenos Aires between the viceroyalty and the fall of Rosas.

fuentes/correo-de-comercio/resumen.texto: Weekly promoted by Belgrano, published between March 3, 1810 and April 6, 1811. It covered economics, education, agriculture and trade, with articles on the usefulness of education and freedom of commerce; after May 1810 it supported the new government.

fuentes/correo-de-comercio/por_que_impor.texto: It is the last expression of the enlightened economic press of the viceroyalty, and it shows Belgrano’s ideas during the months of the revolution.

fuentes/contrato-social/resumen.texto: Treatise published in 1762 that seeks a form of association in which each person, uniting with all, remains free. Through the social pact, each individual gives himself to the community and obeys the general will, from which arises a sovereignty that belongs to the people and cannot be represented or divided. It distinguishes that sovereignty from government, which only executes it, and ends with a chapter on a civil religion.

fuentes/contrato-social/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the most read political works among revolutionaries in France and in the Americas; in Buenos Aires Moreno reissued it in 1810 for schools.

fuentes/contrato-social-edicion-de-moren.texto: On the Social Contract, or Principles of Political Right (Buenos Aires edition of 1810)
Book printed at the Real Imprenta de Niños Expósitos

Edition of a Spanish translation of Rousseau’s Social Contract that Moreno published in 1810, “for the instruction of American youth,” with a prologue of his own. Tradition also credits him with the translation, although his authorship is disputed. In the prologue he explains that he suppressed the chapter on civil religion because the author had had “the misfortune to rave on religious matters.” It was announced as a reading book for schools.
It shows which ideas the most radical sector of the Junta wanted to spread, and also its limits: the sovereignty of the people, but without Rousseau’s religious critique.

fuentes/declaracion-de-derechos-del-homb.texto: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

Declaration approved on August 26, 1789 by the National Constituent Assembly of France. In seventeen articles it states that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, that sovereignty resides in the nation and that the law is the expression of the general will, and it guarantees freedom of opinion and of the press, the presumption of innocence and property.

Its text circulated in America despite the ban: in Bogotá Antonio Nariño printed a translation in 1793 and was convicted for it. Its principles appear in the first statutes and constitutions of the Río de la Plata.

fuentes/de-legibus-suarez/titulo.texto: Treatise on Laws and on God the Lawgiver

fuentes/de-legibus-suarez/resumen.texto: Treatise on the philosophy of law published in Coimbra in 1612. It distinguishes eternal, natural and human law, and holds that the power to make civil laws resides by nature in the political community, which transfers it to the prince through a pact; the king’s power comes from God through the people.

fuentes/de-legibus-suarez/por_que_import.texto: It is the central work of Spanish scholasticism on the origin of power. Manuel Giménez Fernández (1947) and Guillermo Furlong argued that this doctrine, taught in American universities, gave grounds to the idea that sovereignty returned to the peoples in 1810. Tulio Halperin Donghi (1961) objected that a direct line cannot be drawn from Suárez to the arguments of 1810, partly because after the expulsion of the Jesuits the Crown prohibited teaching their doctrines on tyrannicide, and José Carlos Chiaramonte emphasized the weight of modern natural law and the law of nations.

fuentes/estatuto-de-bayona/resumen.texto: Charter granted by Napoleon to Spain on July 6, 1808, after discussing it with an assembly of Spanish notables gathered in Bayonne, in which a few representatives from America took part. It recognized José Bonaparte as king, established Cortes by estates, kept the Catholic religion as the only one, and declared that the kingdoms and provinces of America would have the same rights as the metropolis and their own deputies.

fuentes/estatuto-de-bayona/por_que_impor.texto: It was the first constitutional text for the Spanish monarchy. Neither the Spanish juntas nor the American authorities accepted it, but it obliged its rivals to offer representation to America as well.

fuentes/real-orden-de-la-junta-central-1.texto: Royal order of the Junta Central of January 22, 1809

Decree of the Supreme Central Junta that declared Spain’s dominions in the Indies were not “properly colonies or trading posts,” but an essential and integral part of the monarchy, and called on each viceroyalty and captaincy general to elect a deputy to sit on the Junta. America would thus have some nine members, against more than thirty from the peninsula.
It recognized the equality of Americans in principle but not in representation, one of the grievances taken up by the juntas of 1809 and 1810.

fuentes/constitucion-de-cadiz/titulo.texto: Political Constitution of the Spanish Monarchy (Constitution of Cádiz)

fuentes/constitucion-de-cadiz/soporte.texto: Text of 384 articles, promulgated on March 19, 1812

fuentes/constitucion-de-cadiz/resumen.texto: The first Spanish constitution, known as “la Pepa” because it was promulgated on the feast of Saint Joseph. It defines the Spanish nation as “the union of all Spaniards of both hemispheres,” declares that sovereignty resides essentially in the nation, establishes a moderate monarchy with a division of powers, Cortes elected by indirect suffrage, freedom of the press and the Catholic religion as the only one. Spaniards of African origin were excluded from citizenship and were not counted in calculating the number of deputies, which reduced American representation.

fuentes/constitucion-de-cadiz/por_que_im.texto: It was in force in the areas loyal to the Crown, such as Montevideo, Lima or Upper Peru, between 1812 and 1814 and between 1820 and 1823, and it was the model for several constitutions in Europe and America. Buenos Aires, which did not recognize the Cortes, did not swear it in.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-los-persas/resumen.texto: Document signed on April 12, 1814 by 69 deputies of the ordinary Cortes and delivered to Ferdinand VII on his return from France. It opens by recalling the custom of the ancient Persians of spending several days in anarchy after a king’s death, criticizes the work of the Cortes of Cádiz and calls for restoring the traditional monarchy with Cortes by estates.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-los-persas/por_que.texto: It gave the king the political backing to annul the Constitution of Cádiz a few weeks later.

fuentes/decreto-de-valencia-1814/resumen.texto: Decree signed by Ferdinand VII in Valencia and published in Madrid days later, by which time the leading liberal deputies had already been arrested. It declared null and void the Constitution of 1812 and the decrees of the Cortes, “as if such acts had never taken place,” and restored the king’s absolute power.

fuentes/decreto-de-valencia-1814/por_que.texto: It ended the constitutional path in the empire and hardened the war against the American independence movements.

fuentes/manifiesto-del-rey-1820/titulo.texto: Manifesto of Ferdinand VII to the Nation of March 10, 1820

fuentes/manifiesto-del-rey-1820/resumen.texto: Manifesto published after Ferdinand VII swore the Constitution of 1812, forced to do so by Riego’s pronouncement and uprisings in several cities. It contains the phrase “Let us march frankly, and I first, along the constitutional path.”

fuentes/manifiesto-del-rey-1820/por_que_.texto: It opened the Liberal Triennium (1820–1823) and with it ended preparations to reconquer the Río de la Plata.

fuentes/dialogo-atahualpa-fernando-vii/t.texto: Dialogue between Atahualpa and Ferdinand VII in the Elysian Fields

fuentes/dialogo-atahualpa-fernando-vii/r.texto: Imaginary dialogue that circulated in manuscript in Chuquisaca before the May Revolution of 1809. Atahualpa, the Inca killed by Pizarro, points out to Ferdinand VII, stripped of his throne by Napoleon, that Americans have toward Spain the same right the Spaniards claim against France, and calls on the peoples of America to govern themselves.

fuentes/dialogo-atahualpa-fernando-vii/p.texto: It is one of the first texts to raise independence in Upper Peru. The attribution to Monteagudo is the most widely accepted, although the manuscript is unsigned.

fuentes/carta-de-jamaica/resumen.texto: Letter dated in Kingston on September 6, 1815, addressed to a British resident of the island. Bolívar, in exile, surveys the situation of each region of Spanish America at war, criticizes Spanish rule, analyzes the possible forms of government and foresees the division of the continent into several republics.

fuentes/carta-de-jamaica/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most cited text of Bolívar’s political thought, and an overview of the independence movements at their most difficult moment.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-chile/r.texto: Proclamation of Chile’s independence dated in Concepción on January 1, 1818, signed by Supreme Director Bernardo O'Higgins in Talca on February 2 and solemnly sworn in Santiago on February 12, on the first anniversary of Chacabuco. It declares that Chile and its islands form a free, independent and sovereign state, separate from the Spanish monarchy.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-chile/p.texto: It formalized the outcome of the Army of the Andes campaign, two months before Maipú.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-del-peru/r.texto: Act signed on July 15, 1821 at an open cabildo in Lima, convened at San Martín’s request after the viceroy had left the city. It declares that the general will is the independence of Peru; San Martín proclaimed it in the square on July 28.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-del-peru/p.texto: It formalized the independence of the capital of the former Viceroyalty of Peru, although much of the country remained in royalist hands until 1824.

fuentes/representacion-de-los-hacendados.texto: Brief drafted by Moreno on behalf of José de la Rosa, agent of the landowners, and presented to Viceroy Cisneros in September 1809, when Cisneros was consulting on whether to authorize trade with the British to pay the costs of government. It argues, using the political economy of its time, that opening trade would benefit producers of hides and grain, reduce smuggling and increase revenue; the merchants of the Consulado opposed it. On November 6 Cisneros issued a regulation that allowed that trade on a provisional basis.

It is the main economic writing on the eve of May. Mitre and liberal historiography read it as the economic program of the revolution. Diego Luis Molinari (1914) argued that it did not influence the viceroy’s decision, which sought that temporary permission out of fiscal need, when trade with the British was already practiced de facto.

fuentes/proclama-de-la-junta-1810/titulo.texto: Proclamation of the Provisional Governing Junta of May 26, 1810

fuentes/proclama-de-la-junta-1810/resume.texto: First proclamation of the Junta formed on May 25, addressed to the inhabitants of Buenos Aires and the provinces. It explains that the Junta was formed by the will of the people in view of the situation in Spain, promises to keep these territories for Ferdinand VII and announces that the peoples of the interior will be called on to send deputies.

fuentes/proclama-de-la-junta-1810/por_qu.texto: It shows the language of loyalty to the captive king in which the new government presented itself, whose scope historiography still debates.

fuentes/gazeta-de-buenos-ayres/resumen.texto: Newspaper created by the First Junta to publish its acts, whose first issue appeared on June 7, 1810 under the direction of Mariano Moreno. It printed decrees, war bulletins, correspondence and political articles, and its masthead carried a phrase from Tacitus about the rare happiness of times when one may think what one wishes and say what one thinks. With different editors it appeared until September 1821.

fuentes/gazeta-de-buenos-ayres/por_que_i.texto: It is the main source on government acts between 1810 and 1821.

fuentes/supresion-de-honores-1810/resume.texto: Decree of the Junta of December 6, 1810, drafted by Moreno after an officer, Atanasio Duarte, at a banquet of the Patricios regiment toasted Saavedra as future king and offered a sugar crown to his wife. It removed from the president of the Junta the honors given to the viceroy, made all its members equal and exiled Duarte, because “no inhabitant of Buenos Aires, whether drunk or asleep, should hold impressions against the liberty of his country.”

fuentes/supresion-de-honores-1810/por_qu.texto: It shows the clash between Moreno and Saavedra, which was resolved days later with the admission of deputies from the interior and Moreno’s resignation.

fuentes/plan-de-operaciones/soporte.texto: Manuscript copy held in the General Archive of the Indies

fuentes/plan-de-operaciones/resumen.texto: Document presented as a secret plan of the 1810 Junta. It proposes treating enemies of the revolution with the utmost severity, rising up the Banda Oriental and southern Brazil, expropriating large fortunes to finance the state and seeking the support of Great Britain. Only one copy is known; Eduardo Madero found it in the Archive of the Indies around 1886, and Norberto Piñero published it in 1896 among Moreno’s writings.

fuentes/plan-de-operaciones/por_que_impo.texto: Its authenticity has been disputed since it was published. Paul Groussac considered it apocryphal, while Ricardo Levene, among others, argued that it was Moreno’s. In 2015, in Un plagio bicentenario, Diego Bauso showed that much of the text copies an 1800 French novel, El cementerio de la Magdalena, by Regnault-Warin, which strengthened the position of those who deny that Moreno wrote it.

fuentes/reglamento-para-los-pueblos-de-m.texto: Regulation for the Political and Administrative Government of the Mission Towns

Regulation signed by Belgrano on December 30, 1810, during his campaign to Paraguay, for the Guaraní towns of the former missions. It declares their inhabitants equal to all others, exempts them from tribute for ten years, allows them to trade freely, orders that land be distributed to them, and calls for schools and the abolition of corporal punishment.
It is one of the first revolutionary rules concerning Indigenous peoples, although the war prevented its enforcement.

fuentes/proclama-de-tiahuanaco/soporte.texto: Proclamation and decree of May 25, 1811, also circulated in Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní

fuentes/proclama-de-tiahuanaco/resumen.texto: Proclamation by the Junta’s representative in Upper Peru, read before Indigenous authorities among the ruins of Tiwanaku on the first anniversary of the revolution. It declares Indigenous people free and equal to other inhabitants, announces the end of personal services and of the abuses of caciques and officials, and promises schools and land distribution.

fuentes/proclama-de-tiahuanaco/por_que_i.texto: It expressed the Junta’s intention to win over the Indigenous population of Upper Peru. Less than a month later, the defeat at Huaqui ended Buenos Aires’s presence in the region.

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1811/titulo.texto: Provisional Statute of the Superior Government of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1811/soport.texto: Printed together with the decrees on freedom of the press and individual security

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1811/resume.texto: Statute issued by the First Triumvirate on November 22, 1811, still in the name of Ferdinand VII, after it dissolved the Junta Conservadora. It concentrated power in the Triumvirate and provided for an assembly with periodic renewal. It was published with two decrees of the same government: the decree on freedom of the press, of October 26, and the decree on individual security, of November 23, which prohibited detaining anyone without a written order or holding them without trial.

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1811/por_qu.texto: These were the first texts of a constitutional character issued by the government of Buenos Aires, and they set guarantees that passed into later constitutions.

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1811/leer.0.texto: 1816 reprint of the statute and the 1811 decrees (Internet Archive)

fuentes/tratado-de-pacificacion-1811/tit.texto: Peace Treaty between the Government of Buenos Aires and Viceroy Elío

fuentes/tratado-de-pacificacion-1811/aut.texto: Government of Buenos Aires and Viceroy Elío

fuentes/tratado-de-pacificacion-1811/res.texto: Armistice signed on October 20, 1811 by the Triumvirate and Viceroy Elío, with British mediation. Buenos Aires lifted the siege of Montevideo and recognized Elío’s authority over the Banda Oriental and some towns of Entre Ríos, in exchange for the withdrawal of Portuguese troops.

fuentes/tratado-de-pacificacion-1811/por.texto: The Orientales who followed Artigas experienced it as abandonment, and the army’s withdrawal led to the exodus of the Eastern people.

fuentes/oficio-de-belgrano-sobre-la-band.texto: Belgrano’s Note to the Triumvirate on the Flag

Note in which Belgrano informed the government that, at the Rosario batteries, “it being necessary to raise a flag, and not having one, I had one made white and sky blue in accordance with the colors of the national cockade.” The Triumvirate, which still governed in the name of Ferdinand VII, ordered him in March to conceal it and use the usual flag.
It is the document that dates the creation of the flag and explains its colors by those of the cockade, approved a few days earlier, without mentioning the sky.

fuentes/bando-del-exodo-jujeno/resumen.texto: Proclamation by which Belgrano, facing the advance of the royalist army from Upper Peru, ordered the inhabitants of Jujuy to withdraw with the army, taking their goods and livestock and burning whatever they could not carry, under penalty of execution for anyone who disobeyed or traded with the enemy.

fuentes/bando-del-exodo-jujeno/por_que_i.texto: It is the documentary basis of the Exodus of Jujuy of August 1812.

fuentes/autobiografia-belgrano/resumen.texto: Autobiographical writings in which Belgrano recounts his education in Spain, his work at the Consulado, the British invasions, the revolution, the expedition to Paraguay and the northern campaigns up to the battle of Tucumán. They include his judgments on Spanish commercial policy and on the men of the revolution.

fuentes/autobiografia-belgrano/por_que_i.texto: It is the most extensive direct testimony from one of the members of the First Junta. Mitre used it as the basis of his Historia de Belgrano.

fuentes/archivo-de-belgrano/soporte.texto: Multi-volume documentary collection published by the Museo Mitre since 1913

fuentes/archivo-de-belgrano/resumen.texto: Collection of letters, official notes and papers of Manuel Belgrano preserved in the archive of Bartolomé Mitre, now the Museo Mitre, which he had used for his Historia de Belgrano. It consists mainly of Belgrano’s correspondence with the governments of Buenos Aires and with other leaders during the expedition to Paraguay and the campaigns of the Army of the North.

fuentes/archivo-de-belgrano/por_que_impo.texto: Together with the autobiography, it is the documentary basis of what is known of Belgrano in his own words, and it allows Mitre’s account to be checked against the papers he used.

fuentes/archivo-de-belgrano/leer.0.titul.texto: First volume of the Museo Mitre edition (Internet Archive)

fuentes/memoria-autografa-saavedra/resum.texto: Memoir Saavedra wrote in 1829 about his role between the British invasions and 1811. It recounts the formation of the Patricios, the events of May 1810 from his point of view and his clash with Moreno’s group, which he accuses of wanting to impose its will, and it defends his conduct in the Grand Junta.

fuentes/memoria-autografa-saavedra/por_q.texto: It is the main testimony of the president of the First Junta, written almost twenty years later and with the aim of personal defense.

fuentes/vida-y-memorias-de-mariano-moren.texto: Life and Memoirs of Doctor Mariano Moreno

Biography of Mariano Moreno written by his brother Manuel and published in London in 1812, with a selection of his writings. It presents Moreno as the inspiration of the revolution and his Saavedrist opponents as responsible for his fall.
It fixed the image of Moreno taken up by liberal historiography. It is at once a source and a defense brief of one of the factions of 1810.

fuentes/instrucciones-del-ano-xiii/resum.texto: Instructions given on April 13, 1813 by the congress of the Eastern peoples, meeting at Artigas’s camp opposite Montevideo, to its deputies to the Assembly of the Year XIII. They call for a declaration of absolute independence, a republic, a confederation in which each province holds sovereignty, civil and religious liberty, a division of powers, and that the central government not be seated in Buenos Aires.

fuentes/instrucciones-del-ano-xiii/por_q.texto: Historiography considers it the first federal and republican program of the Río de la Plata. The Assembly rejected the Eastern deputies.

fuentes/oracion-de-abril-artigas/titulo.texto: Artigas’s Opening Address at the Congress of April 1813

fuentes/oracion-de-abril-artigas/resumen.texto: Speech with which Artigas opened the congress of the Eastern peoples on April 5, 1813. He asked them to decide whether to recognize the Buenos Aires Assembly and on what conditions, and said that his authority “emanates from you, and it ceases in your sovereign presence.”

fuentes/oracion-de-abril-artigas/por_que.texto: It is the most cited formulation of the idea of the particular sovereignty of the peoples, which underpinned Artiguism.

fuentes/ley-de-libertad-de-vientres-1813.texto: General Constituent Assembly of the Year XIII

Decree of the Assembly of February 2, 1813 that declared free all children of enslaved women born in the United Provinces from January 31 of that year onward. A regulation of March left those freedmen under the patronage of their mothers’ owners until they came of age. Another decree of February declared free the enslaved people who entered the territory, a rule that was restricted in 1814 in response to complaints from Brazil.

It began the gradual abolition of slavery in the Río de la Plata, which ended only with the Constitution of 1853 and, in Buenos Aires, in 1861. Meanwhile, governments recruited enslaved people for the armies in exchange for their freedom.

fuentes/decreto-de-abolicion-del-tributo.texto: Assembly Decree on Tribute, the Mita and Personal Service of Indigenous People
General Constituent Assembly of the Year XIII

Decree of March 12, 1813 that confirmed the abolition of tribute, ordered by the Junta in 1811, and abolished the mita, the encomienda, the yanaconazgo and the personal service of Indigenous people, whom it declared free men and equal in rights to other citizens.
It legally ended the main institutions of forced Indigenous labor from the colonial period in the territory controlled by Buenos Aires.

fuentes/himno-nacional-argentino/resumen.texto: Song approved by the Assembly of the Year XIII on May 11, 1813 as the only one for the United Provinces, with lyrics by Vicente López y Planes and music by Blas Parera. The original lyrics celebrate the revolution and the victories of Tucumán, Salta and San Lorenzo, and attack “the fierce tyrants” of Spain. A decree of 1900 provided that only the first and last stanzas and the chorus were to be sung at official events, and in 1944 its official version was fixed.

fuentes/himno-nacional-argentino/por_que.texto: It is the main sound symbol of the Argentine state. The changes of 1900 show how it adapted to peaceful relations with Spain.

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1815/titulo.texto: Provisional Statute for the Direction and Administration of the State

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1815/resume.texto: Statute issued on May 5, 1815 by the Junta de Observación after the fall of Alvear. It regulated the election and powers of the Supreme Director, declared the Catholic religion the state religion, recognized individual rights and ordered a general congress to be convened in Tucumán.

fuentes/estatuto-provisional-1815/por_qu.texto: The call for the Congress of Tucumán came from it. Several provinces resisted it because of the powers it gave to Buenos Aires.

fuentes/reglamento-de-tierras-1815/titul.texto: Provisional Regulation of the Eastern Province for the Promotion of Its Countryside and the Security of Its Landowners

fuentes/reglamento-de-tierras-1815/resum.texto: Regulation signed by Artigas on September 10, 1815. It ordered that the lands of emigrants hostile to the revolution, “the bad Europeans and worse Americans,” be divided into estancia lots, giving preference to “the most wretched”: free Black people, zambos, Indigenous people and poor Creoles, who were required to settle them within two months. It also obliged men without land to hire themselves out to an employer.

fuentes/reglamento-de-tierras-1815/por_q.texto: It was in force only briefly, because of the Luso-Brazilian invasion of 1816. Uruguayan historians such as Lucía Sala, Nelson de la Torre and Julio Rodríguez presented it in the 1960s as a revolutionary agrarian reform. Others emphasize its short period of application and its aim of repopulating the countryside and disciplining rural labor.

fuentes/manifiesto-del-congreso-1817/tit.texto: Manifesto to the Nations by the General Constituent Congress of the United Provinces

fuentes/manifiesto-del-congreso-1817/res.texto: Manifesto approved on October 25, 1817 to justify the declaration of independence before other nations. It lists the grievances of three centuries of Spanish rule, from the conquest and the treatment of Indigenous peoples to the commercial monopoly, the exclusion of Creoles from office and the harshness of the war after 1810.

fuentes/manifiesto-del-congreso-1817/por.texto: It is the official justification of independence, designed to win international recognition.

fuentes/reglamento-provisorio-1817/titul.texto: Provisional Regulation for the Direction and Administration of the State

fuentes/reglamento-provisorio-1817/resum.texto: Regulation enacted by Congress on December 3, 1817, already installed in Buenos Aires, to replace the Statute of 1815 while the constitution was being drafted. It reinforced the powers of the Supreme Director, who began to appoint provincial governors.

fuentes/reglamento-provisorio-1817/por_q.texto: It remained in force until the Constitution of 1819, and it was one of the provinces’ grievances against the centralism of the Directorate.

fuentes/el-redactor-del-congreso/soporte.texto: Official Congress newspaper, printed in Buenos Aires because Tucumán had no printing press

fuentes/el-redactor-del-congreso/resumen.texto: Newspaper that summarized the Congress’s public sessions, first in Tucumán and then in Buenos Aires. It was edited by the Franciscan Cayetano Rodríguez and, during the Buenos Aires period, by Vicente López y Planes. It published the debates on independence and the form of government; the secret sessions, as well as much of the debate on monarchy, do not appear in it.

fuentes/el-redactor-del-congreso/por_que.texto: It is the main source on the Congress’s public activity, later complemented by its secret minutes.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1819/titulo.texto: Constitution of the United Provinces of South America

fuentes/constitucion-de-1819/resumen.texto: Constitution enacted by Congress on April 22, 1819. It established a Supreme Director elected by Congress, a Senate with members from the provinces, the army, the clergy and the universities, and a Chamber of Representatives, without defining whether the regime would be republican or monarchical. The Litoral provinces rejected it as centralist.

fuentes/constitucion-de-1819/por_que_imp.texto: Its rejection led to war between the Directorate and the federal caudillos, to the battle of Cepeda, and to the dissolution of the central government in 1820.

fuentes/tratado-del-pilar/autor.texto: Governors of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos

fuentes/tratado-del-pilar/resumen.texto: Treaty signed on February 23, 1820, after Cepeda, by Manuel de Sarratea for Buenos Aires, Estanislao López for Santa Fe and Francisco Ramírez for Entre Ríos. It declares that the nation will be organized as a federation, convenes a congress in San Lorenzo, establishes free navigation of the Paraná and the Uruguay for the signatory provinces and an amnesty. Under a secret agreement, Buenos Aires handed over arms to Ramírez.

fuentes/tratado-del-pilar/por_que_import.texto: It was the first pact among autonomous provinces. Artigas regarded it as a betrayal by Ramírez, and went to war with him.

fuentes/archivo-de-san-martin/titulo.texto: Documents from the San Martín Archive

fuentes/archivo-de-san-martin/soporte.texto: Twelve-volume collection published by the National Centenary Commission

fuentes/archivo-de-san-martin/resumen.texto: Collection of San Martín’s correspondence and papers, kept by his family and later by the Museo Mitre, published between 1910 and 1911. It includes letters to O'Higgins, Guido, Pueyrredón, Godoy Cruz and others, military dispatches and documents from the Chile and Peru campaigns.

fuentes/archivo-de-san-martin/por_que_im.texto: It is the documentary basis of almost everything known of San Martín in his own words.

fuentes/carta-de-lafond/titulo.texto: Letter from San Martín to Bolívar of August 29, 1822 (Lafond letter)

fuentes/carta-de-lafond/soporte.texto: Text known from its publication in French in 1843–1844

fuentes/carta-de-lafond/resumen.texto: Letter in which San Martín, after the Guayaquil meeting, tells Bolívar that he will leave Peru so that Bolívar can finish the war, because he does not believe both of them can be in the country. It is known only from the publication by the French naval officer Gabriel Lafond in his travel memoirs; the original has not survived.

fuentes/carta-de-lafond/por_que_importa.texto: It is the basis of the version according to which San Martín withdrew so as not to divide the independence forces. Venezuelan historians such as Vicente Lecuna held that it was apocryphal; most Argentine historians considered it authentic.

fuentes/ensayo-historia-civil-funes/titu.texto: Essay on the Civil History of Paraguay, Buenos Aires and Tucumán

fuentes/ensayo-historia-civil-funes/resu.texto: The first general history of the Río de la Plata written after the revolution. For the colonial period it follows closely Jesuit chroniclers such as Pedro Lozano, and it ends with an outline of the revolution up to 1816.

fuentes/ensayo-historia-civil-funes/por_.texto: It inaugurated the historiography of the independent country. Its volumes on the colony depend heavily on earlier sources.

personas/pedro-de-cevallos/resumen.texto: Governor of Buenos Aires from 1756 to 1766, he took the Colonia del Sacramento from the Portuguese in 1762. He returned in 1777 as the first viceroy of the Río de la Plata, at the head of the expedition that occupied the island of Santa Catalina and Colonia again, and in November of that year he authorized, by decree, the free inland shipment of merchandise from Buenos Aires to the interior and to Peru. He died in 1778 in Córdoba, Spain, on his way back to the court.

personas/juan-jose-de-vertiz/nombre.texto: Juan José de Vértiz y Salcedo

personas/juan-jose-de-vertiz/resumen.texto: Born in Mérida de Yucatán, he governed Buenos Aires from 1770 and was the second viceroy of the Río de la Plata (1778–1784). During his government the Casa de Niños Expósitos and its printing press were founded, along with the Protomedicato and the Real Colegio de San Carlos; the 1778 padrón was taken, and troops were sent to put down the Andean rebellions of 1780–1781.

personas/marques-de-loreto/nombre.texto: Nicolás Francisco Cristóbal del Campo, Marquis of Loreto

personas/marques-de-loreto/resumen.texto: Third viceroy of the Río de la Plata (1784–1789). During his government the Real Audiencia of Buenos Aires was installed (1785) and the intendancies were put in motion. He sent to Madrid the skeleton of a megatherium found in 1787 near Luján, which Georges Cuvier later studied.

personas/nicolas-de-arredondo/resumen.texto: A military officer who had presided over the Audiencia of Charcas, he was the fourth viceroy of the Río de la Plata (1789–1795). During his government the Consulado de Comercio de Buenos Aires was created (1794).

personas/pedro-melo-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Governor of Paraguay between 1778 and 1785 and viceroy of the Río de la Plata from 1795. He died in Montevideo in April 1797 while organizing the defense of the coast during the war with Great Britain.

personas/antonio-olaguer-feliu/resumen.texto: A military officer who had governed Montevideo between 1790 and 1797 and was left in charge of the viceroyalty after Melo's death (1797–1799). In those years the war with Great Britain cut off trade with Spain, and the Crown allowed trade in ships of neutral countries.

personas/gabriel-de-aviles/nombre.texto: Gabriel de Avilés y del Fierro, Marquis of Avilés

personas/gabriel-de-aviles/resumen.texto: A military officer who fought the Túpac Amaru rebellion in Cusco. Viceroy of the Río de la Plata (1799–1801), he authorized the appearance of the Telégrafo Mercantil and ordered that Guaraní families from the former missions be freed from the communal regime; he later served as viceroy of Peru (1801–1806).

personas/joaquin-del-pino/resumen.texto: A military engineer who governed Montevideo and Chile before becoming viceroy of the Río de la Plata (1801–1804). During his government the Portuguese occupied the Misiones Orientales (1801), the Telégrafo Mercantil kept being published, and the Semanario de Agricultura appeared (1802). He died in office.

personas/rafael-de-sobremonte/resumen.texto: Intendant governor of Córdoba del Tucumán (1783–1797) and viceroy from 1804. Facing the British landing of 1806, he left for the interior with the public treasury, which the British captured at Luján; the open cabildo of August 14 stripped him of military command, and in February 1807 a junta suspended him and had him arrested. His defenders, among them later historians, point out that he was following the planned defense, which called for the treasury to be kept safe; Porteño tradition accused him of fleeing.

personas/santiago-de-liniers/resumen.texto: A French naval officer in the service of Spain. He led the reconquest of Buenos Aires in August 1806 and the defense of July 1807, was acting viceroy from 1807, and withstood Álzaga's uprising in 1809. Replaced by Cisneros, he led the resistance to the May Junta in Córdoba and was executed on its orders at Cabeza de Tigre on August 26, 1810.

personas/baltasar-hidalgo-de-cisneros/re.texto: A naval officer who fought at Trafalgar. The Junta Central appointed him viceroy of the Río de la Plata in 1809; in November of that year he provisionally allowed trade with the British. Deposed in May 1810, he was sent to the Canary Islands with the judges of the Audiencia.

personas/francisco-javier-de-elio/resume.texto: Governor of Montevideo from 1807, in 1808 he formed a junta that refused to recognize Liniers. The Regency appointed him viceroy of the Río de la Plata based in Montevideo (1811); the Buenos Aires Junta did not recognize him, and he returned to Spain at the end of that year. In 1814 he backed, from Valencia, Ferdinand VII's return to absolutism, and the liberals executed him in 1822.

personas/carlos-iii/resumen.texto: King of Spain from 1759, previously king of Naples. He drove the Bourbon reforms in America: he expelled the Jesuits (1767), created the viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (1776–1777), issued the regulation on free trade (1778) and the ordinance on intendants (1782).

personas/carlos-iv/resumen.texto: King of Spain between 1788 and 1808, he left the government in the hands of Manuel Godoy. He abdicated in favor of his son Ferdinand after the Aranjuez riot (March 1808), and in May, at Bayonne, he ceded his rights to Napoleon. He lived in exile in Italy and died in Naples in 1819.

personas/fernando-vii/nacimiento.lugar.texto: Royal Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial

personas/fernando-vii/resumen.texto: King of Spain from the Aranjuez riot (1808); at Bayonne he renounced the crown and was held in France until 1814, while the juntas of Spain and America governed in his name. On his return he annulled the Constitution of Cádiz and restored absolutism; he had to swear to it in 1820, after Riego's pronunciamiento, and annulled it again in 1823 with French help. He never recognized the American independences.

personas/manuel-godoy/resumen.texto: Favorite of Charles IV and his first secretary of state from 1792, he continued to direct Spanish policy until 1808. His alliance with France (1796) led to wars with Great Britain that cut off trade with America, and the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1807) allowed French troops to cross Spain. He fell in the Aranjuez riot and died in Paris.

personas/napoleon/resumen.texto: Emperor of the French (1804–1814 and 1815). In 1808 he obtained at Bayonne the renunciation of Charles IV and Ferdinand VII and gave the crown of Spain to his brother Joseph. The lack of a king recognized in the Spanish empire was the starting point of the juntas of Spain and America.

personas/jose-bonaparte/resumen.texto: Eldest brother of Napoleon, king of Naples and, from 1808, king of Spain as Joseph I. Neither the Spanish juntas nor the authorities in America recognized him; he left Spain after the defeat at Vitoria (1813).

personas/jose-de-galvez/resumen.texto: Visitor general of New Spain (1765–1771) and secretary of the Indies from 1776. He directed the Bourbon reforms in America: the creation of the viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, the free trade of 1778, and the intendancy system.

personas/rafael-del-riego/resumen.texto: An army officer gathered in Andalusia to reconquer the Río de la Plata. On January 1, 1820, he pronounced at Las Cabezas de San Juan for the Constitution of 1812, which Ferdinand VII had to swear to, and the expedition never sailed. He was hanged in Madrid in 1823, after the return of absolutism.

personas/carlota-joaquina/resumen.texto: Daughter of Charles IV and wife of the regent John of Portugal, she arrived in Brazil with the Portuguese court in 1808. She claimed the regency of the Spanish dominions in America while her brother Ferdinand VII was held captive, and a group of Porteño Creoles, among them Belgrano and Castelli, supported that proposal in 1808 and 1809.

personas/juan-vi-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Regent and, from 1816, king of Portugal, he moved the court to Rio de Janeiro in 1808 in the face of the French invasion. He ordered the occupation of the Banda Oriental in 1816 and in 1821 annexed it as the province of Cisplatina.

personas/lord-strangford/resumen.texto: British minister to the Portuguese court in Rio de Janeiro between 1808 and 1815. He mediated among Buenos Aires, Montevideo and Portugal, promoted the 1812 armistice that withdrew the Portuguese from the Banda Oriental, and in 1815 received Alvear's request for a British protectorate.

personas/rousseau/resumen.texto: Philosopher born in Geneva. In The Social Contract (1762) he grounded political legitimacy in a compact by which everyone submits to the general will, and he held that sovereignty belongs to the people. His books were banned in the Spanish empire but circulated in the Río de la Plata, and Mariano Moreno had an edition of The Social Contract printed in Buenos Aires in 1810.

personas/francisco-suarez/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Granada, professor at Coimbra. In De legibus (1612) and Defensio fidei (1613) he argued that political power comes from God through the community, which transfers it to the ruler, and he admitted resistance to a tyrant. Part of the historiography considers him a source of the arguments of the 1810 juntas; another part disputes that filiation.

personas/miguel-gorman/resumen.texto: Irish physician who arrived in the Río de la Plata with Cevallos's expedition. He was the first protomédico of the viceroyalty from 1780 and, with Cosme Argerich, organized the medical school that began operating in 1801.

personas/cosme-argerich/resumen.texto: Porteño physician trained in Barcelona. He taught at the medical school of the Protomedicato from 1801 and, after 1810, organized medical care for the revolutionary army.

personas/felix-de-azara/resumen.texto: Aragonese military engineer sent in 1781 to demarcate the boundaries with Portugal under the Treaty of San Ildefonso. For twenty years he traveled through Paraguay and the Río de la Plata, describing its fauna and peoples in Voyages in South America (1809), and in 1801 he wrote a memoir on the rural state of the Río de la Plata.

personas/manuel-jose-de-lavarden/resumen.texto: Porteño poet and lawyer. His tragedy Siripo premiered around 1789 at the Ranchería theater and does not survive complete; his Ode to the Majestic Paraná River was published in the first issue of the Telégrafo Mercantil (1801).

personas/francisco-cabello-y-mesa/resume.texto: Spanish military officer and writer who had edited the Diario de Lima (1790) in Lima under the pseudonym Jaime Bausate y Meza. In Buenos Aires he founded and directed the Telégrafo Mercantil (1801–1802), the first printed newspaper of the Río de la Plata.

personas/hipolito-vieytes/resumen.texto: Between 1802 and 1807 he published the Semanario de Agricultura, Industria y Comercio. His soap factory, shared with Nicolás Rodríguez Peña, was a meeting place for the Creoles who prepared the revolution of 1810. He was part of Moreno's group that the uprising of April 5 and 6, 1811 removed from government.

personas/tupac-amaru-ii/resumen.texto: Cacique of Surimana, Pampamarca and Tungasuca, in the province of Tinta (Cusco), and a muleteer. In November 1780 he had the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga executed and began the largest Andean rebellion of the 18th century against the repartos forzosos, the mita and the abuses of the corregidores. Captured in 1781, he was executed in Cusco on May 18, after witnessing the death of his wife and other relatives.

personas/micaela-bastidas/resumen.texto: Wife of Túpac Amaru II and one of the leaders of the 1780 rebellion: she handled the logistics and much of the rebels' correspondence. She was executed in Cusco on May 18, 1781.

personas/tomas-katari/resumen.texto: Aymara leader from Chayanta, north of Potosí, who petitioned the Audiencia of Charcas and traveled to Buenos Aires to ask Viceroy Vértiz to recognize him as cacique and to curb abuses in the collection of tribute. His imprisonment set off the Chayanta rebellion in 1780; he died in January 1781 at the hands of those who were taking him prisoner.

personas/tupac-katari/resumen.texto: Aymara leader who in 1781 besieged the city of La Paz for about six months, in two successive sieges. Troops sent from Charcas and Buenos Aires lifted the siege; betrayed by one of his own men, he was executed by quartering in November 1781.

personas/bartolina-sisa/resumen.texto: Wife of Túpac Katari and a leader in the siege of La Paz in 1781. Captured that year, she was executed in La Paz in September 1782.

personas/juan-bautista-tupac-amaru/resum.texto: Half-brother of Túpac Amaru II. Sentenced after the rebellion, he spent almost forty years in prison, most of them in Ceuta; once released, he arrived in Buenos Aires in 1822, where he published his memoirs, The Long Captivity under Spanish Rule, and died in 1827.

personas/home-popham/resumen.texto: British commodore who, after the occupation of the Cape of Good Hope, led without orders from London the expedition that took Buenos Aires in 1806. A court-martial reprimanded him in 1807 for leaving his post without authorization.

personas/william-carr-beresford/resumen.texto: British officer who in June 1806 occupied Buenos Aires with about 1,600 men and governed it for 46 days. He surrendered on August 12 to Liniers's forces; held prisoner in the interior, he escaped in 1807 and later reorganized the Portuguese army against Napoleon.

personas/john-whitelocke/resumen.texto: British general who commanded the second invasion of the Río de la Plata (1807). His assault on Buenos Aires on July 5 failed, and on the 7th he signed with Liniers a capitulation by which he also evacuated Montevideo. A court-martial convened at Chelsea expelled him from the army in 1808.

personas/martin-de-alzaga/resumen.texto: Basque merchant, one of the richest in Buenos Aires, and first alcalde of the Cabildo in 1807 and 1808. He organized the resistance to the British occupation and the defense of 1807; on January 1, 1809, he led an uprising to replace Liniers with a junta, which failed. Accused of conspiring against the revolutionary government, he was executed by firing squad in July 1812.

personas/cornelio-saavedra/resumen.texto: Born in Potosí, he commanded the Patricios regiment formed after the first British invasion and backed Liniers in the uprising of 1809. He presided over the First Junta and the Grand Junta; at odds with Moreno's group, he lost power in 1811 and was prosecuted. In 1829 he wrote a memoir on the revolution.

personas/mariano-moreno/resumen.texto: Lawyer trained in Chuquisaca. In 1809 he drafted the Representation of the Hacendados in favor of trade with the British. He was secretary of the First Junta, founded the Gazeta de Buenos Ayres, pushed for the execution of the leaders of the Córdoba resistance, and published an edition of The Social Contract. He left the Junta in December 1810, when the deputies from the interior joined it, and died at sea in March 1811 on his way to London.

personas/castelli/resumen.texto: Lawyer, second cousin of Belgrano and a member of the First Junta. According to the accounts of those present, at the open cabildo of May 22, 1810 he argued that, once the legitimate government of Spain had fallen, sovereignty returned to the people. As the Junta's representative in Upper Peru he had the royalist leaders of Potosí shot, and at Tiahuanaco he proclaimed the equality of Indigenous people (1811); after the defeat at Huaqui he was put on trial and died in 1812, before sentencing.

personas/belgrano/resumen.texto: He studied in Salamanca and Valladolid and from 1794 was secretary of the Consulado of Buenos Aires, where he wrote memoirs on agriculture, industry, trade and education. A member of the First Junta, he led the expedition to Paraguay, designed the flag (1812), and commanded the Army of the North at Tucumán, Salta, Vilcapugio and Ayohuma. In 1816 he proposed to the Congress of Tucumán a monarchy headed by a descendant of the Incas; he died in Buenos Aires on June 20, 1820.

personas/juan-jose-paso/resumen.texto: He studied at the Colegio de Monserrat in Córdoba and earned his law degree in Charcas. At the open cabildo of May 22, 1810, according to the accounts, he answered the fiscal, Villota, that Buenos Aires could act on behalf of the other towns until they were consulted. He was secretary of the First Junta, a member of both triumvirates, and a deputy to the Congress of Tucumán, of which he was secretary on July 9, 1816.

personas/manuel-alberti/resumen.texto: Priest of the parish of San Nicolás de Bari and a member of the First Junta. He died in February 1811, while a member of the Grand Junta.

personas/miguel-de-azcuenaga/resumen.texto: Military officer from Buenos Aires, member of the First Junta and of the Grand Junta until the uprising of April 5 and 6, 1811 removed him from government along with other supporters of Moreno.

personas/domingo-matheu/resumen.texto: Catalan merchant and member of the First Junta, in charge of supplying weapons and uniforms to the army. He left a diary of the events of those years.

personas/juan-larrea/resumen.texto: Catalan merchant and member of the First Junta. Removed from government in April 1811, he was a deputy to the Assembly of the Year XIII and Minister of Finance under Director Posadas, who financed Brown's squadron.

personas/gregorio-funes/resumen.texto: Dean of the cathedral of Córdoba. As a deputy for Córdoba, in December 1810 he pushed for the incorporation of the deputies from the interior into the Junta, which formed the Grand Junta. He wrote the Essay on the Civil History of Paraguay, Buenos Aires and Tucumán (1816–1817).

personas/domingo-french/resumen.texto: One of the leaders, with Antonio Beruti, of the armed groups that pressed the Cabildo in May 1810. He commanded the squad that executed Liniers at Cabeza de Tigre and was exiled after the uprising of April 1811; later he fought in the Banda Oriental.

personas/antonio-beruti/resumen.texto: One of the leaders, with Domingo French, of the groups that pressed the Cabildo in May 1810. He was exiled after the uprising of April 1811 and later served in the army of independence. He was the brother of the chronicler Juan Manuel Beruti.

personas/juan-manuel-beruti/resumen.texto: Employee of the viceregal administration and later of that of Buenos Aires, brother of Antonio Beruti. For decades he recorded the city's events in his Curious Memoirs, one of the most used sources on the British invasions and the revolution.

personas/nicolas-rodriguez-pena/resumen.texto: Partner of Vieytes in the soap factory where the Creoles who prepared the revolution met. He sat on the Second Triumvirate (1812–1814) and died in exile in Santiago de Chile.

personas/feliciano-chiclana/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer and military officer. He was intendant governor of Salta in 1810 and a member of the First Triumvirate (1811–1812).

personas/manuel-de-sarratea/resumen.texto: Member of the First Triumvirate (1811–1812). He led the second siege of Montevideo until Artigas confronted him; as an envoy in Europe he negotiated in 1815 a project to crown a son of Charles IV in the Río de la Plata. Governor of Buenos Aires in 1820, he signed the Treaty of Pilar.

personas/bernardo-de-monteagudo/resumen.texto: Born in Tucumán and educated in Chuquisaca, he took part in the 1809 revolution in that city; he is credited with the Dialogue between Atahualpa and Ferdinand VII. In Buenos Aires he wrote for the Gazeta, published Martyr or Free, and encouraged the Sociedad Patriótica. He was auditor of the Army of the Andes and San Martín's minister in Peru; he was assassinated in Lima in 1825.

personas/manuel-moreno/resumen.texto: Brother of Mariano Moreno, he accompanied him on the 1811 voyage on which the latter died. In London he published in 1812 the Life and Memoirs of Doctor Don Mariano Moreno, with writings by his brother. He was later a deputy and a diplomat in London.

personas/gervasio-posadas/resumen.texto: Notary of Buenos Aires and uncle of Carlos María de Alvear. He sat on the Second Triumvirate and was the first Supreme Director (January 1814 to January 1815): he armed Brown's squadron, which made it possible to take Montevideo, and declared Artigas a traitor and outlawed him.

personas/carlos-maria-de-alvear/resumen.texto: He arrived from Europe with San Martín in 1812 and led the Lautaro lodge. He presided over the Assembly of the Year XIII, took Montevideo in June 1814, and was Supreme Director in 1815; that year he wrote to Lord Strangford offering to place the provinces under British protection. He fell in April 1815, after the Fontezuelas mutiny, and years later commanded the army in the war with Brazil.

personas/jose-rondeau/resumen.texto: Military officer born in Buenos Aires and raised in Montevideo. He led the second siege of Montevideo and the Army of the North, which was defeated at Sipe Sipe (1815). He was Supreme Director in 1815, in absentia, and again between 1819 and 1820; his defeat at Cepeda dissolved the central government. He later served as provisional governor of Uruguay (1828–1830).

personas/ignacio-alvarez-thomas/resumen.texto: Born in Arequipa. At the head of the troops that rose at Fontezuelas, he brought about Alvear's fall in 1815, and he governed as interim Supreme Director in place of Rondeau until April 1816; under his government the Provisional Statute of 1815 was enacted, which convened the Congress of Tucumán.

personas/antonio-gonzalez-balcarce/resum.texto: He fought in the British invasions. He commanded the Junta's troops that won at Suipacha (1810), the first victory of the revolutionaries, and was interim Supreme Director between April and July 1816.

personas/juan-martin-de-pueyrredon/resum.texto: He organized mounted volunteers against the British occupation of 1806. He was governor of Córdoba and president of the Audiencia of Charcas (1810–1811), a member of the First Triumvirate, and Supreme Director between 1816 and 1819, when he backed San Martín's campaign to Chile. His government did not confront the Luso-Brazilian invasion of the Banda Oriental, which Artigas's supporters reproached him for as complicity.

personas/vicente-lopez-y-planes/resumen.texto: He wrote a poem on the defense of 1807 and the lyrics of the “Marcha patriótica,” which the Assembly of the Year XIII approved on May 11, 1813 as the anthem of the United Provinces. He was provisional president in 1827 and governor of Buenos Aires in 1852.

personas/blas-parera/resumen.texto: Spanish musician born in Murcia to Catalan parents and raised in Mataró, who settled in Buenos Aires. He composed the music of the patriotic song with lyrics by Vicente López y Planes (1813); he returned to Spain in 1818 and died in Mataró.

personas/mariquita-sanchez/resumen.texto: Porteña who in 1804–1805 sued before the viceroy to marry her cousin Martín Thompson against her family's wishes. Her house was a political and literary salon; tradition places there the first time the patriotic song was sung, in 1813, but no document from that year records it.

personas/maria-remedios-del-valle/resume.texto: Afro-Porteña woman who accompanied the Army of the North from 1810 as an auxiliary and combatant, and who lost her husband and sons in the war. In July 1828, after a petition begun in 1827, the Buenos Aires Junta de Representantes granted her the pay of an infantry captain, and in 1829 she was promoted to sergeant major; tradition says Belgrano had named her captain during the northern campaign.

personas/francisco-narciso-de-laprida/re.texto: Deputy for San Juan who presided over the Congress of Tucumán on July 9, 1816, when independence was declared. He died in 1829 in Mendoza, during the war between Unitarians and Federalists.

personas/tomas-de-anchorena/resumen.texto: Deputy for Buenos Aires at the Congress of Tucumán, where he opposed the proposal for an Inca monarchy. A cousin of Juan Manuel de Rosas, he later served as his minister.

personas/justo-santa-maria-de-oro/resume.texto: Dominican friar, deputy for San Juan at the Congress of Tucumán. In the debate over the form of government, he argued that before declaring a monarchy the peoples had to be consulted first. He was the first bishop of Cuyo.

personas/jose-mariano-serrano/resumen.texto: Deputy for Charcas at the Congress of Tucumán and, with Juan José Paso, one of its two secretaries, who signed the act of independence. He later presided over the assembly that declared Bolivia's independence in 1825.

personas/pedro-domingo-murillo/resumen.texto: President of the Junta Tuitiva formed in La Paz after the uprising of July 16, 1809. Defeated by Goyeneche's troops, he was hanged in La Paz on January 29, 1810. The phrase about “the torch I leave burning” is attributed to him by tradition.

personas/jose-manuel-de-goyeneche/resume.texto: Military officer from Arequipa whom the Seville Junta sent in 1808 to the Río de la Plata and Peru. He crushed the La Paz junta (1809) and defeated the Buenos Aires army at Huaqui (1811), for which he received the title of Count of Guaqui.

personas/pio-tristan/resumen.texto: Military officer from Arequipa in the royalist army, a cousin of Goyeneche. He commanded the troops defeated at Tucumán (1812) and Salta (1813), where he capitulated and swore with his soldiers never again to fight against the United Provinces. He was interim viceroy of Peru for a few days after Ayacucho (1824).

personas/joaquin-de-la-pezuela/resumen.texto: Commander of the royalist army in Upper Peru who defeated Belgrano at Vilcapugio and Ayohuma (1813) and Rondeau at Sipe Sipe (1815). Viceroy of Peru from 1816, he was deposed by his own officers in 1821, while San Martín advanced on Lima.

personas/jose-de-la-serna/resumen.texto: Commander of the royalist army in Upper Peru from 1816, whose troops occupied Salta and Jujuy in 1817. In 1821 he displaced Pezuela and became the last viceroy of Peru; he was taken prisoner at Ayacucho (1824).

personas/eustoquio-diaz-velez/resumen.texto: Major general of the Army of the North under Belgrano: he led the retreat from Jujuy in 1812 and fought at Tucumán and Salta.

personas/guemes/resumen.texto: Military officer from Salta who fought in the British invasions and at Suipacha. Governor of Salta from 1815, he organized the defense of the northern frontier against the successive royalist incursions from Upper Peru, with gaucho militias. Wounded by a royalist party in the city of Salta, he died on June 17, 1821.

personas/juana-azurduy/resumen.texto: Born near Chuquisaca, she fought with her husband Manuel Ascencio Padilla in the guerrillas of Upper Peru. Director Pueyrredón gave her the rank of lieutenant colonel in 1816. After Padilla's death, she went to Salta with Güemes; she returned to Chuquisaca and died in poverty in 1862.

personas/manuel-ascencio-padilla/resumen.texto: Leader of the La Laguna guerrilla, east of Chuquisaca, together with his wife Juana Azurduy. He died in combat in September 1816, and the royalists displayed his head.

personas/ignacio-warnes/muerte.lugar.texto: El Pari (Santa Cruz de la Sierra)

personas/ignacio-warnes/resumen.texto: Porteño military officer whom Belgrano named governor of Santa Cruz de la Sierra in 1813. He waged war against the royalists there and died in the battle of El Pari in November 1816.

personas/juan-antonio-alvarez-de-arenale.texto: Military officer born in Spain who took part in the Chuquisaca revolution (1809), led the guerrilla in Cochabamba and Santa Cruz, and commanded the campaigns into the Peruvian highlands in San Martín's expedition. He was governor of Salta between 1824 and 1827.

personas/artigas/resumen.texto: Officer of the Montevideo blandengues who joined the revolution in 1811 and won at Las Piedras. He led the exodus of the Eastern people and, in the Instructions of the Year XIII, upheld independence, the republic and the confederation; as Protector of the Free Peoples he headed the Federal League and issued the land regulation of 1815. Defeated by the Luso-Brazilian invasion and by Francisco Ramírez, he took refuge in Paraguay in 1820 and died there in 1850.

personas/andresito/resumen.texto: Guaraní from the former missions, godson of Artigas, who was commander general of Misiones in the Federal League (1815–1819). He recovered mission towns and fought the Portuguese; captured in 1819, he died in prison in Rio de Janeiro around 1821.

personas/guillermo-brown/resumen.texto: Irish naval officer settled in Buenos Aires. In 1814 he commanded the squadron that took Martín García and defeated the royalist fleet off Montevideo, which led to the surrender of the city. He then commanded the fleet in the war with Brazil and in the Guerra Grande.

personas/hipolito-bouchard/resumen.texto: French naval officer in the service of Buenos Aires, who fought at San Lorenzo (1813). Between 1817 and 1819 he sailed around the world as a privateer of the United Provinces, and in 1818 he attacked Monterey, in Spanish Alta California; he later served in the Peruvian navy.

personas/jose-gaspar-rodriguez-de-franci.texto: Doctor of theology from Córdoba and a member of the Paraguayan junta of 1811. From 1814 he was dictator of Paraguay, and in 1816 he had himself named perpetual dictator; he kept the country isolated from Buenos Aires and its neighbors until his death in 1840. He gave asylum to Artigas from 1820.

personas/fulgencio-yegros/resumen.texto: Paraguayan military officer who fought against Belgrano at Paraguarí and Tacuarí (1811) and presided over the junta formed after May 14 and 15, 1811; he was consul with France in 1813–1814. Accused of conspiring against France, he was executed by firing squad in 1821.

personas/bernardo-de-velasco/resumen.texto: Last Spanish intendant governor of Paraguay. His militias repulsed Belgrano in 1811, and the Paraguayan officers deposed him on May 14 and 15 of that year.

personas/san-martin/resumen.texto: Born in Yapeyú, he was an officer in the Spanish army in the war against Napoleon, and in 1812 he arrived in Buenos Aires, where he formed the Granaderos a Caballo regiment. As governor of Cuyo he organized the Army of the Andes, crossed the Andes in 1817 and won at Chacabuco and Maipú; in 1820 he led the expedition to Peru, proclaimed its independence in 1821, and became its Protector. After the Guayaquil meeting with Bolívar (1822) he gave up command; he died in Boulogne-sur-Mer in 1850.

personas/juan-gregorio-de-las-heras/resu.texto: Commander of the column of the Army of the Andes that crossed by Uspallata. He fought at Chacabuco, Maipú and in Peru, was governor of Buenos Aires (1824–1826), and died in Santiago de Chile.

personas/bernardo-ohiggins/resumen.texto: Son of the viceroy of Peru Ambrosio O'Higgins. A Chilean patriot leader defeated at Rancagua (1814), he went to Mendoza and joined the Army of the Andes. After Chacabuco he was Supreme Director of Chile (1817–1823) and signed the 1818 declaration of independence; he died in Lima.

personas/jose-miguel-carrera/resumen.texto: Governed Chile between 1811 and 1813. After Rancagua he went to Mendoza, where he clashed with San Martín and O'Higgins; later allied with the Litoral caudillos, he was executed by firing squad in Mendoza in 1821.

personas/mariano-osorio/resumen.texto: Royalist commander who reconquered Chile at Rancagua (1814) and in March 1818 surprised San Martín's army at night at Cancha Rayada; he was defeated at Maipú weeks later.

personas/thomas-cochrane/resumen.texto: British naval officer who from 1818 commanded Chile's squadron. He carried San Martín's expedition to Peru (1820) and captured the frigate Esmeralda at Callao; he clashed with San Martín and later served Brazil and Greece.

personas/simon-bolivar/resumen.texto: Leader of the independence of Venezuela and New Granada and president of Gran Colombia. He met San Martín at Guayaquil in 1822 and ended the war in Peru, where his lieutenant Sucre won at Ayacucho (1824).

personas/antonio-jose-de-sucre/resumen.texto: Venezuelan general, Bolívar's lieutenant, who won at Pichincha (1822) and at Ayacucho (1824). He convened the assembly of Upper Peru that declared Bolivia's independence in 1825, and he was its president until 1828.

hechos/expedicion-de-cevallos-1776/resum.texto: The largest expedition Spain sent to the Río de la Plata, with some 9,000 soldiers and more than a hundred ships according to the most cited figures, left Cádiz in November 1776 under Pedro de Cevallos. In February 1777 it occupied the island of Santa Catalina, off Brazil, and in June the Colonia del Sacramento, whose fortifications he ordered demolished; peace came with the Treaty of San Ildefonso.

hechos/creacion-del-virreinato-del-rio-d.texto: Creation of the viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

Charles III created the viceroyalty provisionally on August 1, 1776, for Cevallos's expedition, and made it permanent by royal decree of October 27, 1777. It joined, with its capital in Buenos Aires, the governorships of the Río de la Plata, Paraguay, Tucumán, Cuyo and Upper Peru with Potosí, whose silver began to leave through Buenos Aires.

hechos/primer-tratado-de-san-ildefonso/r.texto: Spain and Portugal signed on October 1, 1777 a preliminary boundary treaty: the Colonia del Sacramento and the Misiones Orientales were left to Spain, and the island of Santa Catalina returned to Portugal. The commissions charged with marking the frontier worked for years without finishing.

hechos/auto-de-libre-internacion/titulo.texto: Cevallos's decree of free inland trade

hechos/auto-de-libre-internacion/resumen.texto: In November 1777 Cevallos authorized that merchandise legally arriving in Buenos Aires could be taken to the interior, to Chile and to Peru. The measure directed the trade of Upper Peru toward the port of Buenos Aires.

hechos/reglamento-de-comercio-libre/resu.texto: On October 12, 1778 the Crown allowed direct trade between a series of ports in Spain and America, among them Buenos Aires, without going through the fleet system. Legal traffic through the port of Buenos Aires grew in the following decades, although trade with other nations remained prohibited except under wartime permits.

hechos/padron-de-1778/resumen.texto: By order of the Crown, Viceroy Vértiz had censuses of the viceroyalty's population taken in 1778, which classified inhabitants by their “quality”: Spaniards, Indians, mestizos, mulattoes and Blacks. The census of the city of Buenos Aires recorded some 24,000 inhabitants, of whom nearly 7,000 were listed as Black or mulatto, free or enslaved; the figures depend on each enumerator's criteria.

hechos/creacion-de-las-intendencias/resu.texto: The ordinance of January 28, 1782, and its adjustments of 1783 divided the viceroyalty into eight intendancies, headed by officials appointed by the king with powers of justice, finance, policing and war. Those of Córdoba del Tucumán and Salta del Tucumán replaced the old governorship of Tucumán and are the antecedent of the provinces of the interior.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-casa-de-ninos-exp.texto: Founding of the Casa de Niños Expósitos
Viceroy Vértiz founded on August 7, 1779 a house for the abandoned newborns of Buenos Aires, financed in part by the printing press he had brought from Córdoba.

hechos/instalacion-de-la-imprenta-de-nin.texto: Installation of the Royal Press of the Casa de Niños Expósitos

The press the Jesuits had kept at the Colegio de Monserrat in Córdoba was moved to Buenos Aires and began work in 1780 for the benefit of the Casa de Niños Expósitos. It was the official press of the viceroyalty and of the first patriot governments.

hechos/fundacion-del-protomedicato/titul.texto: Founding of the Protomedicato of the Río de la Plata

hechos/fundacion-del-protomedicato/lugar.texto: Protomedicato del Río de la Plata

hechos/fundacion-del-protomedicato/resum.texto: On August 17, 1780, Vértiz created the Protomedicato tribunal, presided over by Miguel O'Gorman, to license physicians, surgeons and apothecaries and to oversee public health, instead of depending on the protomedicato of Lima.

hechos/escuela-de-medicina-1801/titulo.texto: First medical school of Buenos Aires
