hechos/escuela-de-medicina-1801/lugar.texto: Protomedicato del Río de la Plata

hechos/escuela-de-medicina-1801/resumen.texto: After a royal order of 1798 approved the Protomedicato and medical teaching, the first regular medical courses in Buenos Aires began in 1801, taught by Miguel O'Gorman and Agustín Eusebio Fabre; Cosme Argerich joined in 1802. Its professors and students treated the wounded of the British invasions and the armies of independence.

hechos/fundacion-del-real-colegio-de-san.texto: Founding of the Real Colegio de San Carlos
Real Colegio de San Carlos (today the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires)

Vértiz, still governor, opened the Reales Estudios de San Carlos in 1772 in the former Jesuit college of Buenos Aires, and in 1783, already viceroy, he founded the Real Convictorio Carolino, with boarding. It was the city's main center of study until the university was founded in 1821.

hechos/fundacion-del-teatro-de-la-ranche.texto: With Vértiz's authorization, a permanent theater opened in 1783 in the Ranchería, near the Manzana de las Luces, for the benefit of the Casa de Niños Expósitos. It operated until a fire destroyed it in 1792.

hechos/megaterio-de-lujan/resumen.texto: In 1787 the Dominican friar Manuel de Torres unearthed on the banks of the Luján River the skeleton of a large extinct mammal, which Viceroy Loreto sent to Madrid. It was assembled at the Royal Cabinet of Natural History, and Georges Cuvier, working from drawings sent from Madrid, described it in 1796 under the name Megatherium.

hechos/creacion-del-consulado-de-buenos-.texto: Creation of the Consulado of Buenos Aires

A royal decree of January 30, 1794, created the Consulado, a commercial tribunal and promotional board for the merchants of Buenos Aires, with Manuel Belgrano as secretary. Besides judging commercial disputes, in 1799 it opened schools of navigation and drawing, which the Crown ordered closed a few years later.

hechos/aparicion-del-telegrafo-mercantil.texto: On April 1, 1801, the first issue of the Telégrafo Mercantil came out in Buenos Aires, directed by Francisco Antonio Cabello y Mesa. It was followed by Vieytes's Semanario de Agricultura (1802–1807) and, in 1810, Belgrano's Correo de Comercio.

hechos/rebelion-de-chayanta/resumen.texto: The Aymara of Chayanta, north of Potosí, rose in 1780 over the imprisonment of Tomás Katari, who had petitioned the Audiencia of Charcas and the viceroy of Buenos Aires against abuses in the collection of tribute. Katari died at the hands of his captors in January 1781, and his brothers continued the rebellion until that year.

hechos/cerco-de-la-paz-1781/titulo.texto: Siege of La Paz by Túpac Katari

hechos/cerco-de-la-paz-1781/resumen.texto: Between March and October 1781 the Aymara forces of Túpac Katari and Bartolina Sisa besieged La Paz in two sieges, during which a large part of the city's population died of hunger and violence. Columns sent from Charcas and Buenos Aires, under Ignacio Flores and José de Reseguín, lifted the sieges; Túpac Katari was executed in November.

hechos/repercusion-de-las-rebeliones-and.texto: The Andean rebellions in the viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

The rebellions of Túpac Amaru, Tomás Katari and Túpac Katari obliged Viceroy Vértiz to send troops and money to Upper Peru and reached Tucumán, where in 1781 there was an uprising on the Jujuy frontier. After the repression, the Crown abolished the corregidores' forced repartos and extended the intendancy system.

hechos/conquista-de-las-misiones-orienta.texto: In 1801, during the War of the Oranges between Spain and Portugal, militiamen from Rio Grande do Sul occupied the seven Guaraní towns east of the Uruguay River. The Treaty of Badajoz did not return them, and they remained with Portugal and later with Brazil.

hechos/batalla-de-trafalgar/resumen.texto: On October 21, 1805, Nelson's British fleet destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet off Cape Trafalgar. Spain lost much of its navy, and its communication with America was left at the mercy of the British; one of the Spanish commanders was Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros.

hechos/motin-de-aranjuez/resumen.texto: Between March 17 and 19, 1808, a tumult of soldiers and residents, encouraged by the partisans of Prince Ferdinand, brought about Godoy's fall and Charles IV's abdication in favor of his son, who reigned as Ferdinand VII.

hechos/abdicaciones-de-bayona/resumen.texto: In May 1808, at Bayonne, Ferdinand VII returned the crown to his father, and Charles IV ceded it to Napoleon, who handed it to his brother Joseph. For most Spaniards and Americans the renunciations were void because they had been forced, and the kingdom was left without a recognized king present.

hechos/guerra-de-la-independencia-espano.texto: It began with the uprising of May 2, 1808, in Madrid against French troops and continued with the formation of juntas in the Spanish provinces, which governed in the name of Ferdinand VII. With British and Portuguese help, the Spaniards expelled the French in 1813–1814.

hechos/junta-suprema-central/resumen.texto: The Spanish provincial juntas formed a Junta Central in September 1808, which governed in the name of Ferdinand VII and was recognized in America. In January 1809 it declared that the American dominions were an integral part of the monarchy and called them to elect deputies; in January 1810, facing the French advance in Andalusia, it dissolved and handed power to a Regency Council.

hechos/consejo-de-regencia/titulo.texto: Regency Council of Spain and the Indies

hechos/consejo-de-regencia/resumen.texto: Created on January 31, 1810, on the Isla de León by the Junta Central before it dissolved, it governed in the name of Ferdinand VII and convened the Cortes. The news of the fall of the Junta Central, which reached Buenos Aires in May 1810, set off the May Revolution, and the Buenos Aires Junta did not recognize the Regency.

hechos/cortes-de-cadiz/resumen.texto: The general and extraordinary Cortes opened on September 24, 1810, on the Isla de León and then sat in Cádiz, besieged by the French. They declared that sovereignty resided in the nation, abolished the Inquisition and seigniorial rights, decreed freedom of the press, and suppressed the Indigenous tribute (1811) and the mita (1812). The American deputies, many of them substitutes chosen among Americans living in Cádiz, demanded equal representation and freedom of trade, with little success.

hechos/promulgacion-de-la-constitucion-d.texto: Promulgation of the Constitution of Cádiz

On March 19, 1812, the Cortes promulgated the first Spanish constitution, “la Pepa.” It was sworn in the loyal American cities, among them Montevideo, Lima and those of Upper Peru; Buenos Aires, which did not recognize the Cortes, did not apply it.

hechos/restauracion-absolutista-1814/tit.texto: Ferdinand VII annuls the Constitution of Cádiz

hechos/restauracion-absolutista-1814/res.texto: Returning from France, and with the support of the deputies of the Manifesto of the Persians and of General Elío, Ferdinand VII signed in Valencia the decree of May 4, 1814, which annulled the Constitution and the work of the Cortes. The liberal deputies were arrested, and the dispatch of troops against the independentists of America was prepared.

hechos/pronunciamiento-de-riego/titulo.texto: Riego's pronunciamiento and the end of the expedition to the Río de la Plata

hechos/pronunciamiento-de-riego/resumen.texto: An army of some 20,000 men had been gathering in Andalusia since 1819 to reconquer the Río de la Plata. On January 1, 1820, Lieutenant Colonel Rafael del Riego pronounced at Las Cabezas de San Juan for the Constitution of 1812; after other uprisings, Ferdinand VII swore to it in March, and the expedition never sailed.

hechos/virreinato-de-pedro-de-cevallos/r.texto: First viceroy of the Río de la Plata, he governed from Buenos Aires after taking Santa Catalina and the Colonia del Sacramento. He issued the decree of free inland trade (1777) and handed over command to Vértiz in June 1778.

hechos/virreinato-de-juan-jose-de-vertiz.texto: Viceroyalty of Juan José de Vértiz

Second viceroy. He founded the Casa de Niños Expósitos, the printing press, the Protomedicato and the Real Convictorio Carolino, carried out the 1778 census, set up the intendancies and sent troops against the Andean rebellions of 1780–1781.

hechos/virreinato-de-marques-de-loreto/t.texto: Viceroyalty of the Marquis of Loreto

hechos/virreinato-de-marques-de-loreto/r.texto: Third viceroy. During his government the Real Audiencia de Buenos Aires was installed (1785), the first intendancies operated, and the megatherium found in Luján was sent to Madrid.

hechos/virreinato-de-nicolas-de-arredond.texto: Fourth viceroy. During his government the Consulado de Comercio de Buenos Aires was created (1794), with Manuel Belgrano as secretary.

hechos/virreinato-de-pedro-melo-de-portu.texto: Viceroyalty of Pedro Melo de Portugal
Fifth viceroy. He governed during Spain’s alliance with France and the start of the war with Great Britain, and died in Montevideo in 1797 while organizing the defense of the coast.

hechos/virreinato-de-antonio-olaguer-fel.texto: Sixth viceroy, in charge of the government since Melo’s death. The British blockade cut off trade with Spain, and the Crown authorized trade in ships of neutral countries, which favored Buenos Aires merchants and North American vessels.

hechos/virreinato-de-gabriel-de-aviles/t.texto: Viceroyalty of the Marquis of Avilés

hechos/virreinato-de-gabriel-de-aviles/r.texto: Seventh viceroy. He authorized the Telégrafo Mercantil and ordered that part of the Guaraní people of the former Jesuit missions be freed from the community regime; in 1801 he became viceroy of Peru.

hechos/virreinato-de-joaquin-del-pino/re.texto: Eighth viceroy. During his government the Portuguese occupied the Misiones Orientales and the Semanario de Agricultura appeared; he died in office in April 1804.

hechos/virreinato-de-rafael-de-sobremont.texto: Ninth viceroy. His government ended with the British invasions: he lost military command at the cabildo abierto of August 14, 1806, and was suspended and arrested by a junta in February 1807.

hechos/virreinato-de-santiago-de-liniers.texto: Tenth viceroy, interim. Head of the defense of 1807, he governed with the support of the criollo militias; he faced the Montevideo junta of 1808 and Álzaga’s uprising of 1809, and handed command to Cisneros in mid-1809, in Colonia del Sacramento.

hechos/virreinato-de-baltasar-hidalgo-de.texto: Viceroyalty of Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros

Eleventh viceroy, appointed by the Junta Central. He provisionally opened trade with the British (November 1809), sent troops against the Chuquisaca junta, while the La Paz junta was being suppressed by forces of the viceroy of Peru, and was deposed in May 1810, when it became known that the Junta Central had fallen.

hechos/virreinato-de-francisco-javier-de.texto: Viceroyalty of Francisco Javier de Elío

Last viceroy of the Río de la Plata, appointed by the Regency based in Montevideo. The Buenos Aires Junta did not recognize him; Elío declared war on it in February 1811, signed the armistice in October and returned to Spain in November.

hechos/primera-invasion-inglesa/resumen.texto: A British force of about 1,600 men under Beresford, brought by Popham from the Cape, landed at Quilmes on June 25, 1806 and occupied Buenos Aires on the 27th. Viceroy Sobremonte withdrew toward Córdoba, and the treasure captured at Luján was exhibited in London. Liniers, with troops gathered in Montevideo and city volunteers, retook Buenos Aires on August 12.

hechos/cabildo-abierto-del-14-de-agosto-.texto: Two days after the reconquest, a cabildo abierto convened under pressure from residents and troops asked that military command pass to Liniers. Sobremonte had to accept it: it was the first time in the Río de la Plata that a cabildo abierto limited a viceroy’s authority.

hechos/formacion-de-las-milicias-urbanas.texto: Formation of the Buenos Aires militias

Fearing a new attack, in September 1806 militia units were formed by origin: Patricios (porteños), Arribeños (from the interior), Húsares, units of Catalans, Biscayans and Galicians, and companies of pardos and morenos. Officers were elected by the troops, and the criollo units, with Cornelio Saavedra at the head of the Patricios, became a political force.

hechos/toma-de-montevideo-1807/resumen.texto: A British force under Samuel Auchmuty took Montevideo by assault on February 3, 1807 and held it until September. During the occupation The Southern Star, a bilingual newspaper, was published there.

hechos/deposicion-de-sobremonte/resumen.texto: After the fall of Montevideo, a war council made up of the Audiencia and the Cabildo suspended Viceroy Sobremonte on February 10, 1807 and placed him under arrest. It was the first time authorities of the Río de la Plata removed a viceroy.

hechos/segunda-invasion-inglesa/titulo.texto: Second British invasion and defense of Buenos Aires

hechos/segunda-invasion-inglesa/resumen.texto: A British army of about 8,000 men under John Whitelocke landed at Ensenada de Barragán at the end of June 1807. On July 5 its columns entered the streets of Buenos Aires and were repulsed by the militias and residents firing from the rooftops, with hundreds killed on each side according to the official reports; on the 7th Whitelocke signed with Liniers the evacuation of the Río de la Plata, including Montevideo.

hechos/consejo-de-guerra-a-whitelocke/re.texto: Between January and March 1808 a court-martial meeting in the Chelsea Hospital tried Whitelocke for the failure at Buenos Aires and the capitulation. It found him guilty and dismissed him from the army.

hechos/junta-de-montevideo-1808/resumen.texto: On September 21, 1808 an open cabildo in Montevideo formed a junta presided over by Governor Elío, which disavowed Liniers’ authority out of suspicion of his French origin. It recognized the Junta de Sevilla and dissolved in 1809, when Viceroy Cisneros arrived.

hechos/carlotismo/resumen.texto: Carlota Joaquina, sister of Ferdinand VII and based in Rio de Janeiro, claimed the regency of the Spanish dominions in America. In Buenos Aires some criollos, such as Belgrano, Castelli, Vieytes and Saturnino Rodríguez Peña, supported her for a time, seeing in her a path to self-government; the project faded in 1809 under British and Portuguese opposition.

hechos/asonada-de-alzaga/resumen.texto: On January 1, 1809 the alcalde Martín de Álzaga and Spanish militia units tried to replace Viceroy Liniers with a junta, like the one in Montevideo. Saavedra’s Patricios and other criollo units backed Liniers; the Spanish battalions were disbanded and the ringleaders exiled to Patagones.

hechos/revolucion-de-chuquisaca/resumen.texto: On May 25, 1809 the Audiencia de Charcas, supported by lawyers and university students, removed President García Pizarro, accused of wanting to hand the territory over to Carlota Joaquina. The movement, in which Monteagudo and Arenales took part, was carried out in the name of Ferdinand VII and was suppressed in December by troops sent by Cisneros.

hechos/revolucion-de-la-paz/resumen.texto: On July 16, 1809 a movement led by Pedro Domingo Murillo deposed the authorities of La Paz; a few days later a Junta Tuitiva presided over by Murillo was formed. Troops sent from Peru by Viceroy Abascal, under Goyeneche, defeated it in October, and Murillo and other leaders were hanged in January 1810.

hechos/apertura-del-comercio-1809/resume.texto: With the treasury empty, Viceroy Cisneros asked in 1809 whether to allow trade with the British, allies of Spain against Napoleon. Moreno defended opening trade in the Representación de los Hacendados, and the Consulado opposed it; on November 6 Cisneros authorized that trade on a provisional basis and with customs duties.

hechos/cabildo-abierto-del-22-de-mayo-de.texto: Convened after the fall of the Junta Central was confirmed, it gathered about 250 leading residents. According to the accounts of those present, Bishop Lué and prosecutor Villota defended the continuity of the viceroy, and Castelli and Paso argued that authority returned to the people; the majority voted that Cisneros should cease and that the Cabildo form a government. On the 24th the Cabildo created a junta presided over by Cisneros himself, who resigned that night in the face of opposition from the militias and from the groups led by French and Beruti.

hechos/primera-junta/resumen.texto: On May 25, 1810, in response to a petition signed by about four hundred residents and military men, the Cabildo accepted a Provisional Governing Junta presided over by Saavedra, with Paso and Moreno as secretaries and Castelli, Belgrano, Azcuénaga, Alberti, Matheu and Larrea as members. It swore to keep the territory for Ferdinand VII, sent expeditions to the interior, to Paraguay and to Upper Peru, banished the viceroy and the oidores (Audiencia judges), and founded the Gazeta. Mitre and liberal historiography saw loyalty to the king as a “mask” for independence; later authors, such as Halperin Donghi and Chiaramonte, interpret it as part of an autonomist project that was still open.

hechos/leyendas-de-la-semana-de-mayo/tit.texto: What is documented and what is legendary about May Week

hechos/leyendas-de-la-semana-de-mayo/res.texto: The Cabildo’s records and contemporary testimonies show the pressure of groups of residents and militiamen led by French and Beruti, not the crowd with umbrellas that the 20th-century school prints spread. The phrase “the people want to know what it is all about” does not appear in the records and comes from tradition. There is also no document showing that in May 1810 blue and white cockades were handed out: the cockade in those colors was approved by the Triunvirato in February 1812, at Belgrano’s request.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-biblioteca-public.texto: Founding of the Biblioteca Pública de Buenos Aires
Biblioteca Pública de Buenos Aires (today the Biblioteca Nacional)
The Junta decreed on September 7, 1810 the creation of a public library, announced by Moreno in the Gazeta, which opened in 1812. It is the origin of the Biblioteca Nacional.

hechos/ejecucion-de-liniers/titulo.texto: Córdoba counterrevolution and execution of Liniers

hechos/ejecucion-de-liniers/resumen.texto: In Córdoba, Liniers, Governor Gutiérrez de la Concha and Bishop Orellana organized resistance to the Junta, but their troops scattered before the expedition sent from Buenos Aires. The Junta ordered them shot; since the commander of the expedition did not carry out the order, Castelli carried it out on August 26, 1810 at Cabeza de Tigre with a firing squad under French, and only the bishop was spared.

hechos/junta-grande/resumen.texto: On December 18, 1810 the Junta incorporated the deputies who had arrived from the interior, as Dean Funes had requested; Moreno, who opposed it, resigned. The enlarged Junta created provincial juntas (February 1811) and was dominated by Saavedra until the defeat at Huaqui weakened it; in September 1811 it delegated the executive power to a triumvirate and, as the Junta Conservadora, was dissolved by the triumvirate in November.

hechos/asonada-del-5-y-6-de-abril-de-181.texto: On the night of April 5 to 6, 1811, troops and people from the outskirts, summoned by Saavedra’s supporters, occupied the plaza and presented a petition to the Junta. Supporters of Moreno, among them Azcuénaga, Larrea, Vieytes and Rodríguez Peña, were removed from government, and French and Beruti were exiled.

hechos/primer-triunvirato/resumen.texto: Formed on September 23, 1811 by Feliciano Chiclana, Manuel de Sarratea and Juan José Paso, with Bernardino Rivadavia as the most influential secretary. It dissolved the Junta Conservadora, issued the Estatuto provisional and the decrees on freedom of the press and individual security, signed the armistice with Elío, and ordered Belgrano to fall back before the royalist advance, an order he disobeyed at Tucumán.

hechos/motin-de-las-trenzas/resumen.texto: On December 6 and 7, 1811, soldiers and noncommissioned officers of the Patricios regiment rose up in their barracks against the order to cut their braids and against the replacement of their commanders. The Triunvirato put down the mutiny, had ten sergeants, corporals and soldiers executed by firing squad on December 11 as ringleaders, and stripped the regiment of the name Patricios and of the number 1 it had held since the English invasions.

hechos/conspiracion-de-alzaga/resumen.texto: In July 1812 the Triunvirato denounced a conspiracy of Spanish merchants led by Martín de Álzaga to overthrow it with support from Montevideo. After summary trials, Álzaga and more than thirty men, among them military officers, friars and merchants, were executed within a few days; their bodies were displayed in the plaza and their property was confiscated.

hechos/revolucion-del-8-de-octubre-de-18.texto: After the victory at Tucumán, won against the orders of the government, the Granaderos de San Martín regiment and other troops, together with the Lautaro lodge and the Sociedad Patriótica, occupied the plaza and forced the Cabildo to replace the First Triumvirate. The Second Triumvirate, formed by Paso, Nicolás Rodríguez Peña and Antonio Álvarez Jonte, called the General Constituent Assembly.

hechos/segundo-triunvirato/resumen.texto: It governed from October 1812 to January 1814, under the influence of the Lautaro lodge and Alvear. It convened and accompanied the Assembly of the Year XIII, which in January 1814 concentrated the executive power in a Supreme Director.

hechos/creacion-de-la-bandera/titulo.texto: Creation of the cockade and the flag

hechos/creacion-de-la-bandera/resumen.texto: On February 18, 1812 the Triunvirato approved, at Belgrano’s request, a white and blue cockade, and on the 27th Belgrano raised a flag in those colors at the batteries of Rosario. The government ordered him to keep it put away, because it still acted in the name of Ferdinand VII; Belgrano had it blessed in Jujuy on May 25, 1812. Belgrano’s official letter explains the colors by those of the cockade; the idea that they represent the sky came later, and their origin remains in dispute.

hechos/batalla-de-suipacha/resumen.texto: On November 7, 1810 the Junta’s troops under Antonio González Balcarce defeated the royalists at Suipacha, in southern Upper Peru, days after having been repulsed at Cotagaita. It was the first victory of the revolutionaries and opened Upper Peru to the expedition.

hechos/fusilamientos-de-potosi/resumen.texto: On Castelli’s orders, as representative of the Junta, the intendant Francisco de Paula Sanz, Marshal Vicente Nieto and General José de Córdoba, leaders of the royalist resistance, were shot in the plaza of Potosí on December 15, 1810.

hechos/batalla-de-huaqui/resumen.texto: On June 20, 1811, on the banks of the Desaguadero, Goyeneche’s royalist army defeated the army of the Buenos Aires Junta, which retreated in disorder as far as Jujuy. The defeat ended the first expedition to Upper Peru and weakened the government of the Junta Grande.

hechos/exodo-jujeno/resumen.texto: On August 23, 1812, by Belgrano’s order, the population of Jujuy abandoned the city with the army, taking livestock and goods and burning what they could not carry, so as to leave the royalists advancing from Upper Peru without resources. The retreat continued as far as Tucumán.

hechos/batalla-de-tucuman/resumen.texto: On September 24 and 25, 1812 Belgrano’s Army of the North, which had disobeyed the order to retreat to Córdoba, defeated the royalist army of Pío Tristán on the outskirts of San Miguel de Tucumán. It halted the royalist advance to the south; Belgrano named the Virgin of Mercy general of his army, on whose feast day the battle was fought.

hechos/batalla-de-salta/resumen.texto: On February 20, 1813 Belgrano defeated Tristán at Salta; the royalist army capitulated and its soldiers swore not to fight again against the United Provinces, an oath many did not keep. The northern provinces were free for a time.

hechos/batalla-de-vilcapugio/resumen.texto: On October 1, 1813, during the second expedition to Upper Peru, the royalist army of Joaquín de la Pezuela defeated Belgrano on the pampa of Vilcapugio, north of Potosí.

hechos/batalla-de-ayohuma/resumen.texto: On November 14, 1813 Pezuela defeated Belgrano again at Ayohuma, forcing the Army of the North to abandon Upper Peru. At the start of 1814 San Martín replaced Belgrano in command.

hechos/batalla-de-sipe-sipe/titulo.texto: Battle of Sipe Sipe or Viluma

hechos/batalla-de-sipe-sipe/resumen.texto: On November 29, 1815 Pezuela defeated Rondeau’s army at Viluma, near Sipe Sipe, during the third expedition to Upper Peru. It was the last great expedition of the United Provinces to Upper Peru; from then on the northern frontier was left to the guerrillas and to Güemes.

hechos/republiquetas/resumen.texto: Guerrilla groups, with heavy Indigenous and mestizo participation, resisted the royalists in various areas of Upper Peru after the defeats of the Buenos Aires armies. Among their leaders were Manuel Ascencio Padilla and Juana Azurduy in La Laguna, Ignacio Warnes in Santa Cruz and Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales in Cochabamba; most of these leaders died in combat or were executed.

hechos/guerra-gaucha/resumen.texto: Between 1814 and 1821 gaucho militias from Salta and Jujuy, organized by Martín Miguel de Güemes, resisted several royalist invasions from Upper Peru with a war of ambushes and destruction of resources, which kept the royalists from holding on in the north. Güemes financed the war with forced contributions from Salta’s merchants and landowners, which generated strong local opposition.

hechos/muerte-de-guemes/resumen.texto: On June 7, 1821 a royalist party that entered Salta at night wounded Güemes, who died on June 17 at the Quebrada de la Horqueta. His militias expelled the royalists shortly afterward.

hechos/campana-al-paraguay/resumen.texto: The Junta sent Belgrano to obtain Paraguay’s adherence, but its governor, Velasco, did not recognize it. The Paraguayan militias defeated him at Paraguarí (January 19, 1811) and Tacuarí (March 9), and Belgrano agreed with the Paraguayan leader Manuel Atanasio Cabañas to withdraw his troops.

hechos/independencia-del-paraguay/resume.texto: On May 14 and 15, 1811 Paraguayan officers deposed Governor Velasco and formed a junta that did not subordinate itself to Buenos Aires. In October it signed with the Buenos Aires Junta a treaty of confederation that was not honored, and from 1813 Paraguay was governed as a separate republic.

hechos/batalla-de-las-piedras/resumen.texto: On May 18, 1811 Artigas’s Oriental forces defeated the royalists of Montevideo at Las Piedras, which made it possible to lay siege to the city.

hechos/primer-sitio-de-montevideo/resume.texto: Forces from Buenos Aires and Artigas besieged Montevideo from May 1811. The entry of Portuguese troops in support of Elío and the defeat at Huaqui led the Triunvirato to sign the armistice in October and lift the siege.

hechos/exodo-oriental/resumen.texto: When the siege of Montevideo was lifted, in October 1811, thousands of inhabitants of the eastern countryside followed Artigas to the Ayuí, on the western bank of the Uruguay River, so as not to remain under royalist and Portuguese rule. They stayed there until 1812.

hechos/segundo-sitio-de-montevideo/resum.texto: From October 1812 the troops of Buenos Aires, under Rondeau, and Artigas’s Oriental forces besieged Montevideo again. Artigas withdrew from the siege in January 1814, at odds with Buenos Aires; the city surrendered to Alvear in June 1814, after the defeat of its fleet.

hechos/congreso-de-tres-cruces/resumen.texto: In April 1813 deputies of the Oriental towns met in Artigas’s camp in front of Montevideo. They recognized the Assembly of the Year XIII under conditions and gave their deputies the Instructions of the Year XIII; the Assembly rejected them because of defects in their election.

hechos/combate-naval-del-buceo/resumen.texto: Between May 14 and 17, 1814 the Buenos Aires squadron, equipped by Director Posadas and commanded by Guillermo Brown, defeated the royalist fleet off Montevideo. Without control of the river, the besieged city surrendered to Carlos María de Alvear on June 23.

hechos/liga-de-los-pueblos-libres/resume.texto: Alliance of the Banda Oriental, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones, Santa Fe and, for a time, Córdoba under Artigas’s protection, which defended the sovereignty of each province against the Directorate of Buenos Aires. It dissolved in 1820, after Artigas’s defeat by the Portuguese and his break with Ramírez.

hechos/congreso-de-oriente/resumen.texto: Assembly of deputies of the towns of the Federal League, convened by Artigas in Concepción del Uruguay, then Arroyo de la China, on June 29, 1815. The documents show that it discussed sending a delegation to Buenos Aires to negotiate with the Directorate; no minutes are preserved. One historiographical current holds that independence was declared there, relying on its reading of a letter from Artigas to Pueyrredón of July 1816, but there is no document from 1815 that proves it.

hechos/invasion-luso-brasilena/titulo.texto: Luso-Brazilian invasion of the Banda Oriental

hechos/invasion-luso-brasilena/resumen.texto: Portuguese troops under Carlos Federico Lecor invaded the Banda Oriental in August 1816 and occupied Montevideo in January 1817. Artigas and Andresito resisted until the defeat at Tacuarembó (January 1820); in 1821 the territory was annexed as the Provincia Cisplatina. The Directorate of Buenos Aires did not intervene, something the Artiguistas reproached it for.

hechos/asamblea-del-ano-xiii/resumen.texto: Installed on January 31, 1813, it declared itself sovereign and stopped swearing allegiance to Ferdinand VII, although it did not declare independence or enact a constitution. It sanctioned the freedom of the womb, abolished the tribute, the mita and the encomienda, noble titles, the Inquisition and torture, minted its own currency and approved the patriotic anthem; in 1814 it created the Directorate. It dissolved in April 1815, with the fall of Alvear.

hechos/combate-de-san-lorenzo/lugar.texto: Convent of San Carlos Borromeo (San Lorenzo)

hechos/combate-de-san-lorenzo/resumen.texto: On February 3, 1813 the Granaderos a Caballo regiment of San Martín surprised a royalist landing party that had come from Montevideo beside the convent of San Carlos, on the banks of the Paraná, and repulsed it. The Corrientes soldier Juan Bautista Cabral died of his wounds, and in his report of the combat San Martín attributed to him last words of victory; that Cabral saved him when he was trapped under his horse was told in later accounts, such as Mitre’s, with details that vary.

hechos/directorio-de-posadas/titulo.texto: Directorate of Gervasio Antonio de Posadas

hechos/directorio-de-posadas/resumen.texto: First Supreme Director, appointed by the Assembly in January 1814. He armed the squadron that made it possible to take Montevideo, declared Artigas a traitor and named San Martín governor intendant of Cuyo; he resigned in January 1815.

hechos/directorio-de-alvear/titulo.texto: Directorate of Carlos María de Alvear

hechos/directorio-de-alvear/resumen.texto: Alvear governed between January and April 1815. That year he sent Manuel José García to Rio de Janeiro with letters offering to place the provinces under British protection. The Fontezuelas uprising and the Cabildo of Buenos Aires forced him to resign and leave the country.

hechos/motin-de-fontezuelas/resumen.texto: On April 3, 1815 troops sent by Alvear against Artigas rose up at Fontezuelas, north of Buenos Aires, under Ignacio Álvarez Thomas. Their pronouncement brought about Alvear’s fall and the dissolution of the Assembly.

hechos/directorio-de-alvarez-thomas/resu.texto: The Cabildo elected José Rondeau Supreme Director; Rondeau was at the head of the Army of the North, and Álvarez Thomas governed as interim from April 1815. Under his government the Provisional Statute was enacted and the Congress of Tucumán was convened; he resigned in April 1816 after failing in Santa Fe.

hechos/directorio-de-gonzalez-balcarce/r.texto: Interim Supreme Director between April and July 1816, while the Congress of Tucumán chose a permanent holder. Pueyrredón, elected by the Congress in May, took office in Buenos Aires at the end of July.

hechos/directorio-de-pueyrredon/titulo.texto: Directorate of Juan Martín de Pueyrredón

hechos/directorio-de-pueyrredon/resumen.texto: Elected by the Congress of Tucumán in May 1816, he governed from Buenos Aires until June 1819. He supported the formation of the Army of the Andes and the campaign to Chile, did not confront the Portuguese invasion of the Banda Oriental and fought the federalists of the Litoral; under his government the Reglamento of 1817 and the Constitution of 1819 were enacted.

hechos/directorio-de-rondeau/resumen.texto: Rondeau succeeded Pueyrredón in June 1819 and called on the Armies of the North and of the Andes to confront the federalists of Santa Fe and Entre Ríos. San Martín did not obey, and the Army of the North mutinied at Arequito; Rondeau was defeated at Cepeda in February 1820 and the Directorate disappeared.

hechos/congreso-de-tucuman/resumen.texto: It was installed in San Miguel de Tucumán on March 24, 1816 with deputies from the interior provinces, Buenos Aires and part of Upper Peru; the Banda Oriental, Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Santa Fe, which followed Artigas, sent no deputies. On July 9 it declared independence; on the 19th it added “any other foreign domination” to the formula of the oath and ordered the act printed also in Quechua and Aymara. In 1817 it moved to Buenos Aires, where it issued the Manifesto to the Nations and the Constitution of 1819, and it dissolved in February 1820.

hechos/proyecto-de-monarquia-incaica/res.texto: On July 6, 1816, in a secret session of Congress, Belgrano proposed a constitutional monarchy headed by a descendant of the Incas, as a way to win over the Andean peoples and European recognition. Güemes and several deputies from Upper Peru and the north supported it, and Buenos Aires deputies such as Tomás de Anchorena rejected it. Congress did not approve it, and in 1819 it secretly negotiated the candidacy of a European prince.

hechos/batalla-de-rancagua/resumen.texto: On October 1 and 2, 1814 the royalist army of Mariano Osorio defeated O’Higgins’s Chilean patriots at Rancagua and recovered Chile for the Crown. Thousands of Chileans emigrated to Mendoza, where they joined San Martín’s preparations.

hechos/ejercito-de-los-andes/titulo.texto: Formation of the Army of the Andes

hechos/ejercito-de-los-andes/resumen.texto: San Martín, governor intendant of Cuyo since August 1814, organized an army to cross into Chile with Pueyrredón’s support. It was financed with contributions from the people of Cuyo and from the central government, recruited freed people among the region’s slaves, and trained at the El Plumerillo camp; Fray Luis Beltrán directed the workshops.

hechos/cruce-de-los-andes/lugar.texto: Andes Cordillera (Los Patos and Uspallata passes)

hechos/cruce-de-los-andes/resumen.texto: Between January and February 1817 the Army of the Andes, some 5,000 men, crossed the cordillera by six passes; the main columns followed those of Los Patos, with San Martín, and Uspallata, with Las Heras. The smaller columns distracted the royalists along hundreds of kilometers.

hechos/batalla-de-chacabuco/resumen.texto: On February 12, 1817 the Army of the Andes defeated the royalist army on the Chacabuco slope, north of Santiago. Two days later it entered the capital, and an open cabildo named O’Higgins Supreme Director of Chile.

hechos/independencia-de-chile/resumen.texto: The act of independence, dated January 1, 1818, was proclaimed and sworn in Santiago on February 12, the anniversary of Chacabuco.

hechos/sorpresa-de-cancha-rayada/resumen.texto: On the night of March 19, 1818 the royalist army of Osorio made a surprise attack on the combined army of Chile and the United Provinces, camped near Talca, and scattered it. Las Heras saved part of the infantry, the basis of the reorganization.

hechos/batalla-de-maipu/resumen.texto: On April 5, 1818, on the plains of Maipú, south of Santiago, San Martín defeated Osorio’s army. The battle secured Chile’s independence and made it possible to prepare the expedition to Peru.

hechos/expedicion-libertadora-del-peru/r.texto: On August 20, 1820 an army of some 4,000 men under San Martín set out from Valparaíso with Cochrane’s Chilean squadron, financed mainly by Chile. San Martín had disregarded the Directorate’s order to return with his army to fight the federalists; in April 1820, at Rancagua, his officers confirmed him in command. He landed at Paracas in September and negotiated with the viceroys while extending the war into the highlands.

hechos/independencia-del-peru/resumen.texto: Viceroy La Serna abandoned Lima in July 1821; an open cabildo signed the act of independence on July 15, and San Martín proclaimed it on the 28th. He assumed the office of Protector of Peru on August 3, while the royalists kept the highlands and Upper Peru.

hechos/entrevista-de-guayaquil/resumen.texto: San Martín and Bolívar met alone in Guayaquil on July 26 and 27, 1822, without witnesses or minutes. What was discussed is known from letters and later accounts from both sides, including the letter from Lafond, whose authenticity is disputed. San Martín resigned before the Congress of Peru on September 20 and retired; Bolívar finished the war.

hechos/sancion-de-la-constitucion-de-181.texto: On April 22, 1819 Congress enacted a centralist constitution that did not define the form of government. The Litoral provinces rejected it, and the war between the Directorate and the federalists resumed.

hechos/batalla-de-cepeda-1820/resumen.texto: On February 1, 1820 the federal forces of Estanislao López (Santa Fe) and Francisco Ramírez (Entre Ríos) defeated Director Rondeau in the Cañada de Cepeda. The Cabildo of Buenos Aires dissolved the Congress and the Directorate on February 11, and the city became just another province, without a national government.

hechos/firma-del-tratado-del-pilar/titul.texto: Signing of the Treaty of Pilar

hechos/firma-del-tratado-del-pilar/resum.texto: On February 23, 1820 Sarratea, López and Ramírez signed, in the chapel of El Pilar, a treaty declaring their will to organize a federation, convening a congress and opening the navigation of the rivers to the signatory provinces. Artigas considered it a betrayal, and the war with Ramírez ended with his exile in Paraguay.

hechos/corso-de-bouchard/titulo.texto: Hipólito Bouchard’s voyage around the world

hechos/corso-de-bouchard/resumen.texto: With a letter of marque from the United Provinces, Hipólito Bouchard’s frigate La Argentina sailed around the world between 1817 and 1819, attacking Spanish commerce in Asia and the Pacific. In November 1818 it landed at Monterey, capital of Alta California, and occupied it for several days.

lugares/protomedicato-de-buenos-aires/no.texto: Protomedicato del Río de la Plata

lugares/protomedicato-de-buenos-aires/re.texto: Tribunal created by Viceroy Vértiz on August 17, 1780, with the Irish physician Miguel O’Gorman as protomédico, to examine and license physicians, surgeons and apothecaries and to oversee public health in the viceroyalty; the Crown approved it by royal order of 1798. In 1801 it opened the first school of medicine in Buenos Aires. It operated until 1822, when its functions passed to the university and to other provincial agencies.

lugares/real-colegio-de-san-carlos/nombr.texto: Real Colegio de San Carlos (today the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires)

lugares/real-colegio-de-san-carlos/resum.texto: Vértiz opened the Reales Estudios de San Carlos in 1772 in the former Jesuit college of the Manzana de las Luces, and in 1783 the Real Convictorio Carolino, a boarding school, was founded there. Several men of the revolution studied there, among them Mariano Moreno and Juan José Castelli. Reopened in 1818 as the Colegio de la Unión del Sud, it became the Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires in 1863.

lugares/casa-de-ninos-expositos/resumen.texto: Founded by Viceroy Vértiz on August 7, 1779 in the Manzana de las Luces to receive abandoned newborns. It had a wooden turntable in the wall that allowed a baby to be left without being seen, and it was used until 1891. To sustain it, Vértiz assigned it part of the profits of the printing press he had brought from Córdoba.

lugares/imprenta-de-ninos-expositos/resu.texto: The first permanent printing press in Buenos Aires, installed by Vértiz in 1780 with the press that had belonged to the Jesuit college of Monserrat, in Córdoba, to print proclamations and official documents and to help the Casa de Niños Expósitos with its profits. There the Telégrafo Mercantil, the Gazeta de Buenos Ayres and the edition of the Contrato social of 1810 were printed.

lugares/teatro-de-la-rancheria/resumen.texto: Theater opened in 1783, with permission from Viceroy Vértiz, at the corner of today’s Alsina and Perú streets. Around 1789 the tragedy Siripo, by Manuel José de Lavardén, premiered there. A fire destroyed it in 1792.

lugares/biblioteca-publica-de-buenos-air.texto: Biblioteca Pública de Buenos Aires (today the Biblioteca Nacional)

The First Junta decreed its creation on September 7, 1810 and announced it in the Gazeta, with Mariano Moreno as protector. It was formed with donations and with books from ecclesiastical libraries, and it opened to the public in March 1812 in the Manzana de las Luces. It is today the Biblioteca Nacional Mariano Moreno.

lugares/convento-de-san-carlos/nombre.texto: Convent of San Carlos Borromeo (San Lorenzo)

lugares/convento-de-san-carlos/resumen.texto: Franciscan convent on the banks of the Paraná, near Rosario, begun in 1792 and occupied from 1796. San Martín and the Granaderos a Caballo regiment hid in it before the combat of San Lorenzo, on February 3, 1813, and its refectory served as a field hospital. In 1819 the armistice between Belgrano and Estanislao López was signed there.

lugares/convento-de-santo-domingo-buenos.texto: Basilica and Convent of Santo Domingo (Buenos Aires)

Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary, of the Dominicans, in central Buenos Aires. During the defense of July 1807 a British column took refuge in the convent and ended up surrendering; the church keeps flags taken from the British. In its forecourt is the mausoleum of Manuel Belgrano.

lugares/cabildo-de-montevideo/resumen.texto: Building of the Montevideo cabildo, begun in 1804 facing the Plaza Matriz. It was the seat of city government during the viceroyalty, the patriot siege, Portuguese and Brazilian rule and the first years of independent Uruguay; in front of it, in the Plaza Matriz, the first Uruguayan constitution was sworn in 1830.

lugares/cabildo-de-lujan/resumen.texto: Building of the cabildo of the town of Luján, begun in 1792. In 1806 British troops seized in Luján the funds that Viceroy Sobremonte had taken out of Buenos Aires, and in 1810, according to local history, its cabildo was the first to recognize the First Junta. Today it forms part of the Luján museum complex.

lugares/cabeza-de-tigre/resumen.texto: Site in southeastern Córdoba, near today’s Los Surgentes, on the road from Buenos Aires to Upper Peru, where on August 26, 1810 former viceroy Santiago de Liniers and four other leaders of the Córdoba resistance were shot on the orders of the Buenos Aires Junta. Bishop Rodrigo de Orellana, arrested with them, was pardoned because of his status as a cleric.

lugares/el-plumerillo/resumen.texto: Camp set up in 1816 a few kilometers from Mendoza, where San Martín assembled and trained the Army of the Andes. From there the columns set out that crossed the cordillera in January 1817.
